There are several players proven to have Premier League quality – Raul Jimenez and Kieran Trippier foremost among them – or with a fine past record in the Championship like Adam Armstrong, whose signing last January was taken as the first major move towards building a serious second-tier side. Last season was awful but some of the players who held their heads up and had been expected to move do not appear – for now – to be clamouring to leave. The positive choices of Jimenez to return and Andre to stay, when both could surely have found opportunities at higher levels in England or overseas, suggest that a core spirit of unity can exist, a powerful emotion in a demanding Championship programme.

Weaknesses? There are obvious questions. What if the exodus has not been cancelled, just delayed? If any of the seniors who appeared unwanted in May but now might be important components of the Championship challenge do go, can the club do better than last summer's flawed recruitment? Is there enough defensive strength apart from Ladislav Krejci, whose pre-season was limited after the World Cup? Will either of the club's two international goalkeepers end up staying, and if not can another senior keeper be found? The answers to these questions may not become clear until 2 September.

Difference-maker? This time last year, Mateus Mane's abilities were well-known only to those who nurtured him at Rochdale or closely studied the form of Wolves' youth teams. But several months before his departure, Vitor Pereira had identified Mane as a future star, and under Rob Edwards the teenage forward was given the first opportunities to demonstrate that ability. Arguably there were too many opportunities for his age and his season faded out, but he had already shown enough to be the focus of fans' hopes for the future. Through pre-season he has appeared fresh, motivated and refreshingly well-grounded, as if appreciating that a strong Championship season could gold-plate his potential for a major future.

Quiz: How much do you remember about Wolves' 2017-18 season?

It's a new era, the past is the past - Peixoto

Key ins: Danny Imray (Crystal Palace), Ben Whiteman (Preston), Anthony Patterson (Sunderland)

Key outs: Paul Mullin (Rotherham), Jay Rodriguez (released), Andy Cannon (Fleetwood, free)

Expectations? There is no doubt that Wrexham want to be pushing for promotion, particularly having gone so close to securing a play-off spot last season. A top eight finish will likely be viewed as a success given the restructuring of the play-offs, although the Red Dragons will want to push for top six.

Strengths? The squad possesses some real individual talent, including Josh Windass and Callum Doyle, while Kieffer Moore's variety of talents up front make him a real danger in the Championship. Wrexham are also very clinical. Phil Parkinson's side outperformed their expected goals (XG) by 12.21 last season, more than any other second tier side. Maintain that ruthless nature in front of goal and the Red Dragons will have another strong campaign.

Weaknesses? They gave up plenty of chances and efforts on their goal last season. It took time for Parkinson to find a settled back three in 2025-26, and injuries at wing-back certainly didn't help the team's balance. The hope, and probably even expectation, is that Wrexham will improve defensively having had a year to acclimatise to the division.

Difference-maker? Danny Imray, who was the club's first signing of the summer, has the profile to slot in seamlessly on the right flank. The injury record of last season's first-choice wing-backs Liberato Cacace and Issa Kabore was poor, but Imray has chalked up 76 appearances during loan spells across the past two seasons combined.

'Big decisions' for Wrexham as Falchener targeted

Wrexham sign Sunderland goalkeeper Patterson

title: Titans & underdogs - League One club-by-club preview
description: BBC Sport correspondents assess the strengths and weaknesses of all 24 teams competing in League One this season.
fullText:
League One has some titans joining the fray this season.

Leicester City lifted the Premier League trophy a decade ago but now they return to the third tier for the first time since 2009, while Sheffield Wednesday are back to kick off a new era under brand new ownership.

But with such recent, rich history comes mammoth expectation and for the Foxes in particular, nothing else will do other than promotion.

While for a club like last season's League Two champions Bromley, who have already reached a new height in securing promotion to League One for the first time, the pressure is off.

Could this be another year of the underdogs?

Follow your League One club this 2026-27 season

Key ins: Dan Sweeney (Stevenage, free), Steve Seddon re-signing for the new season

Key outs: Omar Bugiel (Suzhou Dongwu, free)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Keep their heads above water, and keep improving.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? Defensively the Dons can be tough to breakdown.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Far too streaky, runs of wins will almost certainly be followed by a long barren drought.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Marcus Browne - technically brilliant, he's a key man in all good things they do.

Adam Oxley, BBC Radio Sheffield

Key ins: Cameron McGeehan (Northampton, free), Sam Gale (Gillingham, undisclosed), Clayton Taylor (Newcastle Jets, undisclosed)

Key outs: David McGoldrick (Mansfield, free), Adam Phillips (Bradford, undisclosed), Eoghan O'Connell (Stockport, free)

Expectations? Daniel Stendel has been a popular choice, external to replace Conor Hourihane as head coach this summer. The German has returned to Oakwell hoping to repeat the success he achieved in his first spell when he guided the Reds to the Championship in 2018-19.

Barnsley have a limited budget as the owners aim to operate within their means. A top-half finish would feel like a step in the right direction for the Reds, but the fanbase - who have seen their side play in the second tier for the majority of the club's history - will expect the team to be at least knocking on the door of the play-offs.

Strengths? The focus has been on recruiting young, hungry players to Stendel's high-energy, high-pressing game.

Retaining key midfielders in Patrick Kelly, Luca Connell and Reyes Cleary, coupled with the youthful enthusiasm of the club's new signings, the majority of whom are aged 23 and under, will offer hope that Stendel can mould a team to at least cause problems for the more fancied teams in the division.

Weaknesses? The Reds have lost goals and experience this summer with last season's top three scorers David McGoldrick (18), Davis Keillor-Dunn (16) and Adam Phillips (11) all having departed Oakwell.

Returning midfielder Cameron McGeehan, who previously played at Oakwell in Stendel's first spell, is currently the only player in his 30s in the squad, and a lack of a few experienced heads has historically not served Barnsley well.

Difference-maker? Patrick Kelly is likely to be crucial to any success that Barnsley achieve this year. The 21-year-old got better and better throughout his first campaign with the Reds and ended the season as a full Northern Ireland international, scoring his first goal for his country against France just before this summer's World Cup.

Andy Bayes, BBC Radio Lancashire

Key ins: Jordan Williams (Portsmouth, loan), Dion Charles (Huddersfield, loan), Ilmari Niskanen (Exeter, free), Karoy Anderson (Charlton, undisclosed), Finley Munroe (Middlesbrough, loan)

Key outs: Ashley Fletcher (Huddersfield, free), James Husband (Doncaster, free)

Expectations? To build on the impressive end to last season, when they climbed away from trouble with six wins from their last seven games. If they can start brightly, expectations may begin to rise, although Ian Evatt is at pains to stress that Blackpool have no right to consider themselves challengers simply because of the size of the club.

Strengths? There are plenty of attacking options, but keeping them fit is an issue straight away. They've got great options in midfield, with Albie Morgan back in action after a long absence to complement the talent already there. Signing Karoy Anderson permanently is a big boost. He impressed last season while on loan.

Weaknesses? Injuries. The centre of defence has taken a big hit, with Fraser Horsfall and Michael Ihiekwe both missing the start of the campaign following injuries sustained last term. Likewise, the absence of Dale Taylor in the forward line with a hamstring problem is a huge blow.

Blackpool missed far too many players last season, and this year doesn't look much different.

Difference-maker? Josh Bowler. On his day, he is a Championship-level player, but Blackpool now need a level of consistency from him. In a team that plays three at the back, it can be difficult to get the very best out of an out-and-out wide player, but his goal on the opening day at Grimsby will no doubt give him the confidence to find more.

Key ins: Jake Beesley (Burton Albion, undisclosed), Adam Phillips (Barnsley, undisclosed), Macaulay Gillesphey (Charlton Athletic, undisclosed), Callum Connolly (Stockport County, free), Jon McCracken (Dundee, free)

Key outs: Jenson Metcalfe (Millwall, undisclosed), Max Power (Wigan Athletic, undisclosed), Sam Walker (Watford, undisclosed), Curtis Tilt (Burton Albion, undisclosed)

Expectations? It will take some going to replicate Bradford City's fourth placed finish in League One of last season, particularly given it was their first time back at the level in six years.

The Bantams proved last season that money isn't everything, but with some financial heavyweights now in the division, a successive top six finish may be an unfair expectation for this evolving club. Just outside it may still be considered a 'good' campaign.

Strengths? Recruitment has long been a strength of the football club's rapid rise over the last couple of years. That again could prove dividends from their summer work so far. Their forward line, in particular, looks well stocked with the newly acquired Jake Beesley and Adam Phillps. Add into the mix their impressive home form over that period, Valley Parade could once again prove fortress-like.

Weaknesses? Midfield remains a concern for many supporters. The heartbeat of last season's play-off push was quickly ripped apart with the sizeable sale of Jenson Metcalfe and the surprise departure of captain Max Power.

Whilst the addition of Callum Connolly offers some solution, along with the deeper deployment of new captain Antoni Sarcevic, the Bantams still feel short in the centre-point of their spine.

Difference-maker? One of their own, Bobby Pointon. The ever-flourishing homegrown talent has taken to League One like a duck to water. Still only 22, his goal return has increased season-on-season. We're yet to truly know his ceiling, but his floor continues to rise.

Ryan Matthews, BBC Radio London

Last season: League Two champions

Key ins: Shamal George (Wycombe, free), Kamil Conteh (Bristol Rovers, undisclosed), Jacob Mendy (Peterborough, free), Chanse Headman (Harrogate Town, undisclosed), Deon Woodman (Wealdstone, undisclosed), Victor Adeboyejo (Mansfield, free), Ethon Archer (Luton Town, loan), Richard Taylor (Bolton Wanderers, loan), JJ McKiernan (Lincoln City, undisclosed)

Key outs: Idris Odutayo (Dundee, free), Jude Arthurs (Crawley Town, free), Ben Krauhaus (Brentford, end of loan), Byron Webster (retired), Carl Jenkinson (released), Kyle Cameron (Newport County, free), Sam Long (Salford City, free), Marcus Dinanga (Aldershot Town), Brooklyn Ilunga (Hartlepool Town, free)

Expectations? It is very tricky to define any level of expectations for Bromley this season. Even the most optimistic of Bromley fans wouldn't have dreamed of reaching League One so quickly, so expectations will have to be reasonable - particularly with the level of financial muscle in the league.

A good season for Bromley would be proving that their approach works at the level, with a couple of notable scalps along the way and retaining their place in the division.

Strengths? Bromley are, and have been defined by their superior fitness and robust approach in the last few seasons. Whilst they are no slouches tactically and can outplay teams on their day, Andy Woodman has built a brand of football that is centred around peak physical performance, tall imposing players and set piece excellence.

This, coupled with the incredible team spirit that Woodman has engendered at Bromley will stand them in good stead in the upcoming season.

Weaknesses? A large percentage of the squad are still unproven and untested at this level and whilst the club have moved to address this with their summer recruitment, there is still a question mark as to how they will be able to adapt to League One level.

Specifically, a lack of quality in depth particularly in forward areas could be a limiting factor - club talisman Michael Cheek has confounded expectations in League Two and, whilst you wouldn't bet against him transferring his goalscoring exploits up another level, the burden will have to be shared around.

Difference-maker? Ethon Archer - young winger on loan from Luton Town. Skilful dead ball specialist, League One experience scoring 11 goals in 81 appearances for Cheltenham, three in 23 on loan with Port Vale last season.

Key ins: Curtis Tilt (Bradford, undisclosed), Matty Dennis (Notts County, undisclosed), Corey Addai (Stockport, loan), Gbemi Arubi (Dundalk, undisclosed)

Key outs: Jake Beedley (Bradford, undisclosed), Udoka Godwin-Malife (Reading, undisclosed), Dylan Williams (Motherwell, undisclosed), Terence Vancooten (Stevenage, undisclosed)

Expectations? Even the most optimistic Burton Albion supporter would struggle to make a case for anything other than yet another battle against relegation – and there are few out there when making their season's predictions who have the Brewers anywhere other than the bottom four.

Gary Bowyer masterminded the Great Escape in 2024-25, after arriving at the club when nobody gave them a chance of avoiding the drop. Given the summer the Brewers have had so far, staying up this time around would be the Greatest Escape.

Weaknesses? The major issue Bowyer has is, once again, the size of his squad.

Sixteen of last season's contracted players have been sold or released – including skipper Udoka Godwin-Malife and leading scorer Jake Beesley - and the three loan players who finished the campaign have departed. At the time of writing, just four have been brought in, three on permanent deals and one on loan. The club is going to have to work hard before transfer deadline day to make up the deficit.

Difference-maker? Bowyer gave a categorical 'no' when asked if he expects to have striker Tyreece Shade in his squad come the beginning of September. Charlie Webster's recent injury record might mean he remains until January at least.

Experience is an issue, so the spotlight will be on skipper Curtis Tilt and midfielder George Evans who, between them, account for the vast majority of EFL appearances in the squad as it currently stands.

Mark Johnson, BBC Radio Cambridge

Last season: Third in League Two

Key ins: Gassan Ahadme (Charlton, loan), Callum Perry (Coventry, loan), Isaac Heath (Everton, free)

Key outs: Adam Mayor (end of loan), James Gibbons (Notts County, free)

Expectations? Probably mid-table, although whether it's a comfortable or nervy mid-table remains to be seen. For what it's worth, I suspect the former.

Strengths? Head coach Neil Harris knows the division well and can set up a team with the right shape, mentality and flexibility to surprise a few in the coming season... and he'll relish the role of the underdog.

Shayne Lavery was re-signed after being released at the end of the last season; his return will bring potency and mobility to the front line, but Cambridge will need to wrap him in cotton wool to ensure they can get enough minutes from his beleaguered hamstrings.

Weaknesses? This biggest worry is the depth of the squad. The business they've been able to do so far has been excellent, but signings seem to have dried up at the moment.

This is a concern as several members of the squad will need to have their playing time carefully managed as they are far from bullet proof in terms of injury records. It feels like the squad is about three or four players light, so there's still plenty of work to be done before the transfer window closes.

Difference-maker? Gassan Ahadme is the obvious choice as he's traditional centre forward the club lacked last season (although they did pretty well finding a work-around!).

But for me, Ben Knight has the potential to be one of the most inventive players not just at the club, but in the division.

How one city's high cost of living is putting off footballers

Robbie Andrews, BBC Radio Sheffield

Key ins: Alfie May (Huddersfield, loan), Isaac Hutchinson (Bristol Rovers, undisclosed), Jordan Thomas (Cheltenham, free)

Key outs: Luke Molyneux (Salford, undisclosed)

Expectations? Rovers made a brilliant start to last season, but needed a very good end to avoid relegation. A top half finish is not out of the question with a greater level of consistency.

Strengths? The recruitment of players who have experience for the level, for example defender James Husband and Alfie May, will help Rovers in trying to achieve their aims.

Plus the squad lacked League One experience last season, so they'll be more street wise this time around.

Weaknesses? Belief was viewed to be a big issue for much of last season, so hopefully they won't lack that now. Strength in depth in forward areas might be an issue as there are injury concerns to Frankie Okoronkwo.

Difference-maker? A less heralded summer signing has been Leon Ayinde from Ipswich, but he's looked good in pre-season, never takes a backward step, and always looks to make things happen.

Key ins: Ashley Fletcher (Blackpool, free), Ibane Bowat (Portsmouth, undisclosed), Ethan Brierley (Brentford, undisclosed), Matt Young (Sunderland, loan), Derens Fernandes (Excelsior, undisclosed) and Ilias Bronkhorst (Excelsior, free)

Key outs: Alfie May (Doncaster Rovers, loan), Lee Nicholls (Preston, undisclosed),

Expectations? Ideally, an uninterrupted third successive tilt at promotion, this time without yet another change of manager/head coach in the new year. There has been a notable aim expressed by club decision-makers for the team to prioritise entertainment and avoid predictability.

Strengths? The sheer volume of brand new and as-new recruits (many of whom remain from last summer's staggering intake) over the past 14 months as a whole. The squad appears overstocked in certain positions, so departures should still be expected in the opening weeks.

Weaknesses? Individual talent is unmistakeable, but consistent collaboration has been thin at Huddersfield since relegation from the Championship.

With such an oversized player pool to start with, non-selections will be a long list, so squad harmony might be unusually hard to achieve. To manage such hazards, the addition of Alan Knill's calm experience to the dynamic younger coaching talents of Drury, Jonathan Stead and Co. is a clever strategy.

Difference-maker? For on-the-ball thrills, pacy new winger Derensili Fernandes will be hard to beat. Centre-back Jack Whatmough's recovery from being injured for most of last season could be the essential missing barricade, though much is also expected from Ibane Bowat, signed from Portsmouth.

Jack Rafferty, BBC Radio Leicester

Last season: 23rd in the Championship, relegated

Key ins: Liam Cullen (Swansea, undisclosed), Conor Chaplin (Ipswich, free), Wes Burns (Ipswich, undiscosed), Tommy Watson (Brighton, loan), Admir Bristic (Olimpija Ljubljana, undisclosed)

Key outs: Abdul Fatawu (Ipswich, £20m), Ricardo Pereira (released), Harry Winks (Cagliari, undisclosed), Jordan Ayew (released), Jannik Vestergaard (released), Patson Daka (Hamburg, free)

Expectations? Anything other than an immediate return to the Championship will be considered a failure, ideally as champions.

Given they won the league in their only other season in the third tier, finishing second or below would mark the club's lowest ever league finish. With the squad Russell Martin has assembled, along with some really exciting academy talent, the Blue Army will be hoping for a very successful campaign.

Strengths? Martin appears to have had a really positive transfer window so far. As well as allowing plenty of players to depart, he has added some real talent to his ranks, including a number of players he's worked with before. Players that he trusts and who know his style well.

The club were desperately in need of a striker, and finally landed Bosnian Admir Bristic, on Tuesday. Those additions, combined with some really exciting academy talent, could produce some magic on the pitch.

Weaknesses? The transfer window isn't quite shut yet, which will concern some City fans. There are still plenty of rumours about potential departures, including centre back Harry Souttar, who captained the side in the EFL Cup last week.

Given they've already lost Ben Nelson to an ACL injury, losing another defender without a suitable replacement could leave them very short at the back.

Difference-maker? The obvious answer would be to name one of the new recruits, such as Cullen, Burns or Chaplin who have proven pedigree at this level. The player I'm most excited about is academy product Sammy Braybrooke.

After a couple of successful loans in League Two last season, the lad dubbed the 'Leicester Iniesta' looks more than ready to step up and be a key part of City's promotion push. He, alongside young right back Jayden Joseph, have been the standout players at the end of pre-season, particularly as he made his first senior start for the club in the EFL Cup.

A secret invite and other 'pinch-me' moments before Leicester woke up

Key ins: Jaze Kabria (Grimsby, undisclosed), Nathan Baxter (Watford, undisclosed), Isaac Hayden (QPR, free).

Key outs: Dom Ballard (Bristol City, undisclosed)

Expectations? Improved leadership and character. Higher levels of focus, energy and discipline.

Jaze Kabria to compete to become a third successive Golden Boot winner at the O's following Charlie Kelman and Dom Ballard.

Evidence of the development of a squad capable of staging a serious promotion challenge.

Strengths? This summer the O's have signed an experienced keeper as well as a central defender, two full backs and a defence minded midfielder, which should address the frailties at the back that caused so many problems last season.

Weaknesses? Lack of depth in the squad, there maybe insufficient cover in the case of injuries and suspensions.

Difference-maker? Nathan Baxter, Leyton Orient's first permanent goalkeeper since returning to League One in 2022-23. The 27-year-old should ensure confidence for those in front of him.

Adam Oxley, BBC Three Counties Radio

Key ins: George Johnston (Bolton, undisclosed), Kasey Palmer (Hull, undisclosed), Callum Marshall (West Ham, undisclosed)

Key outs: Milli Alli (Charlton, undisclosed), Elijah Adebayo (released), Jacob Brown (Reading, free)

Expectations? After the strong finish last season, supporters will expect a promotion challenge from the start.

Strengths? Jack Wilshere has fans fully onside after a patchy start, and they have kept key midfielders Jordan Clark and Liam Walsh. Defender George Johnston led Bolton to promotion last season.

Weaknesses? A potential lack of goals so the performance of new striker Callum Marshall could be key.

Difference-maker? Kasey Palmer's arrival on loan last season kick-started the season, with a Wembley win and almost reaching the play-offs. He has now signed on a permanent deal, and Wilshere will be hoping Palmer can reproduce that loan form over a whole season.

Last season: Second in League Two (promoted)

Key ins: Ryan Wintle (Cardiff, free), Sam Nombe (Rotherham, free), Charlie Goode (Stevenage, free)

Key outs: Luke Offord (Crewe Alexandra, free), Aaron Nemane (Rotherham, free)

Expectations? The aim is promotion, the expectation is certainly to be in and around the play-off places come the end of season shake up.

Strengths? Paul Warne – four promotions from the division with Rotherham United and Derby County. MK Dons also have huge strength in depth in midfield. Alex Gilbey, Liam Kelly & Ben Wiles were mainstays of the side promoted last term. The club have added in the close season and feasibly have six players vying for three places.

Weaknesses? Defensively the players are very good but Warne needs to work out if a back three or back four is best suited to the personnel. In addition, at the time of writing there is no seasoned back up goalkeeper.

Difference-maker? Ryan Wintle, Cardiff's player of the year last season knows how to get out of this division and that experience could be vital.

Jake Garner, BBC Radio Nottingham

Key ins: David McGoldrick (Barnsley, free), Michael Smith (Preston North End, free), Liam Thompson (Derby County, undisclosed)

Key outs: Will Evans (Plymouth Argyle, undisclosed), Aaron Lewis (released)

Expectations? Steady progress remains the aim as Mansfield Town prepare for their third season in League One.

Last season's 10th place finish proved they can compete comfortably at this level, and an improved league position, coupled with a good cup run, would represent another successful campaign. A push for the play-offs is not beyond the realms of possibility either!

Strengths? Mansfield have strengthened their attack with the arrivals of proven goalscorers David McGoldrick and Michael Smith, helping address an issue that cost them valuable points last season.

The squad's versatility is also a major asset, with players such as Jordan Bowery and Lucas Akins capable of filling a variety of roles. Bowery especially will probably cover six different roles between now and May.

Weaknesses? The biggest concern is the age profile of the squad and whether key players can stay fit over a long season. Injuries have been a recurring problem for Mansfield in recent years, and several important figures are now in their mid-to-late thirties.

While they still bring a huge amount of quality and experience, there are understandable questions over how they will cope with the demands of another lengthy campaign. That said, age is increasingly just a number in modern football, with McGoldrick's 18 League One goals for Barnsley last season highlighting exactly that.

Difference-maker? McGoldrick will naturally attract plenty of attention, as will goalkeeper Liam Roberts, but if he stays injury free, Tyler Roberts could be the player who truly makes Mansfield tick.

His quality, agility and creativity made an immediate impact after arriving at the club last season, he looks revitalised and he's rediscovered his love for football here. A clever pass, a moment of skill or a clinical finish, there will be plenty of magical Roberts moments as he has the ability and confidence to unlock defences. Very excited to see more of him this season.

Adam Hassell, BBC Radio Nottingham

Last season: Fifth in League Two (promoted via the play-offs)

Key ins: Cal Roberts (Scunthorpe, free), Jack Evans (Harrogate, undisclosed), Ollie Cooper (Swansea, loan)

Key outs: Alassana Jatta (Casa Pia, undisclosed), Matty Dennis (Burton, undisclosed), Tom Iorpenda (end of loan)

Expectations? Notts are back in the third tier for the first time since 2015 and fans will largely be happy with simply staying in the division by the end of the season.

Notts became a very workmanlike team under Martin Paterson last campaign, with individuals arguably largely playing above their abilities; the Magpies will need the same again if they're to compete with some of the big-hitters in League One.

Strengths? Martin Paterson knows how to make his teams hard to beat. They're resilient and dogged and are able to stay in games effectively.

Jack Evans and Dean Campbell coming into the midfield add a grit that should mean Notts are not nice to play against. They'll be aggressive and tenacious and hopefully the team will be effective in its approach.

Weaknesses? To put it simply, where are the goals going to come from? Notts lost three of their four top scorers from last season over the summer, and rumours continue to circulate about where Jodi Jones' future lies. If he leaves, Notts will have lost 58 of their 74 league goals from last season, most notably Alassana Jatta.

Without signing a new out-and-out forward, they could really struggle to find the net regularly.

Difference-maker? All that being said above, they have a player in Cal Roberts who is able to provide a bit of magic from the number 10 position.

He's also never played as high as League One before, so it could be a risk to be dependent on him for those moments of class. But if he's able to do it at this level, he could help turn losses into draws and draws into wins and hopefully score the goals to keep Notts in League One by the end of the season.

Last season: 22nd in the Championship, relegated

Key outs: Will Lankshear (loan ended), Myles Peart-Harris (loan ended), Przemysław Płacheta (Austin FC, free)

Expectations? The arrival of Aaron Ramsey, external was taken as a signal that Oxford would be going all out for an instant return to the Championship. But even before his feet were under the desk, the club was placed under a temporary transfer embargo, expected to effectively be in place until January.

The aim will be to stay in contention until then. Four wins from four in pre-season, and with Ramsey getting Oxford back to playing a more energetic, positive brand of football, the mood has lightened a little. Predictions of how the U's will fare, understandably, vary wildly.

Strengths? Oxford have implemented a retention policy which means they've (so far) hung onto most of the contracted top talent, virtually all with Championship experience.

There have been some impressive performances in pre-season from young players who were being blocked last year by a bloated squad of senior players and the difficulties of blooding them in a relegation battle.

Weaknesses? Ramsey has to maintain harmony when at least some of the players he will wish to deploy might have expected their futures to lie elsewhere. He also has to hope that a lack of depth isn't exposed by any injury crisis, with Oxford looking vulnerable in a couple of positions.

Their only summer signing Frankie Kent (Hearts, free) will miss most of the season with a knee injury.

Difference-maker? Wales international Mark Harris scored 19 goals for Oxford in League One in 2023-24. Oxford need him to recapture that sort of form.

Oxford's fight to prove they are not a crisis club

PFA starts legal proceedings over League One salary cap

Ben Stevenson, BBC Radio Cambridgeshire

Key ins: Thomas O'Connor (Wrexham, free), Evan Weir (Walsall, free), Owura Edwards (Colchester, free), Harrison Jones (Sunderland, undisclosed), Collin Andeng-Ndi (Southend, undisclosed)

Key outs: Archie Collins (released), Kyrell Lisbie (Millwall, undisclosed), Tom Lees (Harrogate, free), Cian Hayes (Rochdale, undisclosed), Abraham Odoh (Salford, undisclosed)

Expectations? The aim from the club's hierarchy is to challenge for promotion, but given Posh have finished 18th for the past two seasons and are restricted by the current financial position, many fans would be content with avoiding another flirt with relegation.

Strengths? It might be a cliche to say Posh's biggest asset right now is their manager Luke Williams, but there is more than an element of truth in that statement.

When he was appointed last October, he took a side bottom of the table and turned them into play-off contenders. Their promotion dreams were dashed when his young, injury hit squad hit a wall. The hope this season is that there are less injuries and Williams is able to recruit more players suited to his style of play.

Weaknesses? Having lost some of their best players from last season, some of the fanbase have been quick to bemoan the lack of proven quality coming in to replace them.

Injuries have undoubtably hampered Posh for the past couple of seasons, whilst a lack of experience and physical presence were also issues that haven't really been addressed yet.

Difference-maker? Peterborough United's two stand out players play at opposite ends of the pitch.

Goalkeeper Alex Bass is arguably the best goalkeeper the club has had for many years. Striker Harry Leonard has shown he has the potential to follow in the footsteps of some of the great forwards to have played at London Road in recent times. Both players will be key if Peterborough are to achieve their target.

Brent Pilnick, BBC Sport England

Key ins: Alex Mitchell (Charlton, undisclosed), Wes Harding (Millwall, free), Murphy Cooper (QPR, undisclosed)

Key outs: Lorent Tolaj (Bristol City, undisclosed)

Expectations? Having been bottom of the table in November the Pilgrims finished the season in eighth place, and for a brief spell on the final day were sixth. Argyle have kept the bulk of the squad and fans will hope for a play-off place as a minimum.

If they can start this season the way they ended the last, who is to say a top two place is not out of reach?

Strengths? The continuity from last season's squad is key - loanees Alex Mitchell and Wes Harding have joined permanently while only out-of-contract goalkeeper Conor Hazard and top-scorer Lorent Tolaj have left, the latter for a fee in excess of £4m.

Weaknesses? Argyle need more attacking cover. With Tolaj's departure and a significant injury to Michael Baidoo, coupled with injuries to Caleb Watts and Tegan Finn, Plymouth look light going forward.

Difference-maker? Bim Pepple. The Canadian striker started last season slowly, but by the end had earned his first senior international call-up after scoring 15 goals in his final 20 appearances. With Tolaj leaving he is now the focal point of the Argyle attack and the club need him to hit the ground running.

Hartridge says abuse from fans 'went too far'

Tim Dellor, BBC Radio Berkshire

Key ins: Josh Stokes (Bristol City, loan), Udoka Godwin-Malife (Burton, undisclosed), Kyreece Lisbie (Colchester, undisclosed), Jacob Brown (Luton, free)

Key outs: Derrick Williams (retired), Matt Ritchie (retired), Kelvin Ehibhatiomhan (AC Horsens, undisclosed)

Expectations? Modest expectations right now. Reading are starting their fourth consecutive season in League One. With the squad as it is right now, in all probability they will be starting a fifth this time next year. The most optimistic fans will be hoping Reading sneak into the play-offs.

Strengths? Jack Marriott staying fit is central to success. If he plays more than 40 games, Reading will expect to finish in the top six. The issue is his fitness record in recent seasons. Getting more than 30 games from him will be good progress.

Lewis Wing in central midfield dictates everything, and is frequently head and shoulders above his team-mates, bringing real quality to games. Expect big seasons from Paudie O'Connor and Joel Pereira, as well. These experienced players are Championship quality.

Weaknesses? Right now there's a worrying lack of depth. The last few seasons has seen a string of injured players missing crucial games, and the club ought to fear the worst and hope for the best when it comes to planning for this campaign.

Right now a couple of injuries in defence and attack would leave the squad looking extremely flimsy. Recruiting a robust, athletic striker and central defender will cost money, but would make all the difference.

Difference-maker? This time last year, and the year before, it was Lewis Wing. It's the same answer this time, though Jack Marriott, if he can stay fit, is also a valid answer now.

Couhig targets sustainable Reading and promotion

Rob Staton, BBC Radio Sheffield

Last season: 24th in the Championship, relegated

Key ins: Barry Bannan (Millwall, undisclosed), Louie Barry (Aston Villa, undisclosed), Billy Mitchell (Millwall, free), Mason Burstow (Hull, loan), Callum Slattery (Motherwell, free)

Key outs: Pierce Charles (Manchester City, undisclosed), Svante Ingelsson (Stoke City, undisclosed)

Expectations? It's hard to say what the "expectations" are. Some will expect promotion because the club is under new ownership and there's a feel good factor around the club.

The reality, though, is this is a squad being built virtually from scratch and whilst some good additions have been brought in, it might not be enough - so far at least - to feel like Wednesday will go up.

Strengths? They have some good footballers. The likes of Bannan, Mitchell, Barry, Slattery, Burstow and Leeds loanee Harry Gray possess a level of technical quality. They can be difference makers on their day.

Plus, keeping the likes of Max Lowe was a big move and captain Liam Palmer won player of the year last time they were in League One.

Weaknesses? Do they have enough grit and 'grown men' type players to battle through League One. Last time Wednesday got out of this division they had Michael Smith and Callum Paterson types. League One isn't like the Championship and you've got to know the league.

Henrik Pedersen, who's under a bit of pressure already after winning only two games last season in an admittedly horrible situation, is also very new to this division.

Difference-maker? When I went to Wednesday's training camp in Hungary, 17-year-old Will Grainger stood out. He looked electric.

Everton wanted him this summer but he signed a new deal. He looks like a tremendous prospect and I wouldn't bet against him developing a role this season. Grainger looks like a player capable of playing at a high level.

'Owls' promotion will be harder than some think'

Key ins: Josh Magennis (Exeter, free), Oliver Sanderson (Fulham, undisclosed), Terry Taylor (Charlton, free), Terence Vancooten (Burton Albion, undisclosed)

Key outs: Charlie Goode (MK Dons, free), Harvey White (Plymouth, free), Dan Sweeney (AFC Wimbledon, free)

Expectations? Wide expectation will be that Stevenage will struggle this season with a limited budget and competing with some of the larger clubs in the division.

Confidence will be high around the club that they can compete as they did last season and use the momentum of reaching the play-off places. Realistically, a top 10 placing would be a huge success.

Strengths? Stevenage have built their success on a solid defence that performs miserly. They also have a phenomenal work-rate through the squad.

Weaknesses? A lack of goals that has been an issue for the past two seasons, could again prove to be their downfall. A lot will be expected from Jamie Reid and new signings Josh Magennis and Ollie Sanderson, but they need to pick up more goals throughout the team.

Difference-maker? Phoenix Paterson. Now in his second season at Stevenage and quite clearly the player that can provide a spark to create goals. A frustrating season last term as he was very much regarded as learning the "Stevenage way". Signs are that he has served his apprenticeship and is ready to kick on.

Mark Crossley, BBC Radio Manchester

Key ins: Oli Whatmuff (Manchester City, loan), Mikael Mandron (St Mirren, free), Harry Wood (Shelbourne, undisclosed), Ryan Glover (Barnet, undisclosed), Eoghan O'Connell (Barnsley, free), Jason Adigun (Chelmsford City, undisclosed)

Key outs: Corey Addai (Burton Albion, loan), Ben Hinchliffe (retired), Joseph Olowu (Leyton Orient, undisclosed), Odin Bailey (Portsmouth, free), Jayden Fevrier (Blackburn Rovers, undisclosed)

Expectations? Despite the departure of two key figures in boss Dave Challinor and director of football Simon Wilson, there is real positivity heading into a new era at Edgeley Park.

County owner Mark Stott has openly admitted that he "didn't enjoy" watching the team last season, even though they only missed out on promotion to Bolton at Wembley. Fans have been told to expect "a different approach" under new boss Jimmy McNulty, who led Rochdale back to the EFL last year.

Strengths? Kyle Wootton has shown he will always be a constant threat in front of goal. Tying Ollie Norwood and Ethan Pye down to new deals was vital this summer. Norwood is now the oldest player at the club and has been handed the armband too. He might be 35 but still has the quality to unlock any defence.

Weaknesses? McNulty has never managed in League One but insists he is "completely ready" for the step up. However, it feels likely it could be a season of transition, as he attempts to implement his methods. Expect lots of possession - but do they have enough match winners?

Difference-maker? On-loan Manchester City goalkeeper Oli Whatmuff has followed McNulty to Edgeley Park from Rochdale, following his heroics at Wembley. He certainly doesn't lack confidence and has been called "a future England number one" by his manager. No pressure.

Josh Watton, BBC Radio Manchester

Key ins: Max Power (Bradford, undisclosed), Sonny Perkins (Leyton Orient, undisclosed)

Key outs: Sam Tickle (Bristol City, undisclosed)

Expectations? It feels like heading into the unknown with Wigan. They have finished 12th or below for the past three seasons, fans see this as a huge underachievement.

Gary Caldwell has made his ambitions clear, he wants to put that run to an end and finish comfortably in the top half, I'm not sure if they have the squad to achieve this on paper, however Caldwell is an expert in working wonders with a lower budget.

Strengths? Max Power has returned to the Latics for a third time, he'll come in and add some much-needed leadership in the middle of the field, that seemed to be lacking last season.

Weaknesses? Firepower up front, Joe Taylor solved that issue last season but it was only a temporary fix. Their second top scorer last season came from midfield, Callum Wright chipped in with seven and he has also left the club after his loan ended. If they are to achieve their goals this season, they really need to solve their issues in front of goal.

At other end, Sam Tickle has been invaluable for Wigan ever since coming into the first team, I imagine having him in goal has saved them around 10 points a season. He has now moved on to Bristol City and leaves a huge gap which has been filled with Joe Walsh, who has huge shoes to fill.

Difference-maker? Sonny Perkins is the new number nine at Wigan and has a lot of weight on his shoulders.

Gary Caldwell has experience in getting the best out of forwards, turning them into 20 goal a season strikers. If he can work his magic again, Perkins may live up to the expectations which were placed on him whilst rising through the West Ham and Leeds United academy.

Sam Avery, BBC Radio Three Counties

Key ins: Conor Hazard (Plymouth Argyle, free), Sam Parker (Swansea City, loan), Silko Thomas (Leicester City, free), Cauley Woodrow (Luton Town, undisclosed), Emre Tezgel (Stoke City, loan)

Key outs: Will Norris (Salford City, free), Declan Skura (Walsall, loan), Fin Back (Released), James Tilley (AFC Wimbledon, loan), Alex Lowry (Motherwell, loan)

Expectations? Fans are generally enthused about the prospect of a full season under Michael Duff, given the upturn in form following his appointment last season. As a result, there is optimism that the play-offs could be within reach. Having said that, it looks like a much tougher League One than last season.

Strengths? Continuity from last season. Before the injuries to some key players in March, the Chairboys were on track for a really strong finish to last season.

Fred Onyedinma, Dan Harvie and Cauley Woodrow were some of Wycombe's top performers in that time and all signed new contracts - or signed permanently in Woodrow's case!

Weaknesses? At the time of writing, Emre Tezgel is the only out and out striker that the club have signed this summer, leaving a lot of pressure on him to fulfil the shortcomings from Wycombe's high expected goal rate last season.

But, the biggest challenge facing the club this season might be the stadium! The terrace has been partially closed for structural repairs, leaving fans concerned about the effect that could have on the home atmosphere.

Difference maker? The obvious pick would be Fred Onyedinma after winning Supporters' and Players' player of last season. But, Ewan Henderson might just be the one to look out for. He was playing well last season until a couple of injuries before the New Year, but has looked really sharp again during pre-season.

You can catch all the action from the opening weekend of the EFL right here on the BBC Sport website with live text coverage across all three days, starting with Wolves v Blackburn Rovers on Friday at 20:00 BST.

title: How Maresca's Man City are shaping up compared with Guardiola side
description: Enzo Maresca has the difficult task of following Pep Guardiola at Manchester City. BBC Sport analyses the new manager's style and tactics from the pre-season games so far.
fullText:
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has no easy task following Pep Guardiola's impressive 10-year act.

For many, his appointment suggests a continuation in tactical approach.

But Maresca, despite clearly being inspired by his former mentor, has his own style and one which we have started to see emerge across City's pre-season.

To understand Maresca's City we need to provide some context about Guardiola's.

Guardiola, by some, is mistakenly thought to be strictly married to a singular approach. While Guardiola had principles he stuck to throughout his career, he did not stick to one system.

These principles included keeping as much of the ball as possible, as far away from his team's goal and as close to the opponent's goal. His game was also founded on the basis of positional play.

Domenec Torrent, a long-time assistant of Guardiola's, offered a nice definition of positional play, describing it as "how you place yourself in relation to others on the field when you have the ball, and where you should be so that you can continue pressing when you lose it".

The coach implements tactics based on the positions of players in the hope of giving their team an advantage.

The end of Torrent's definition highlights another key Guardiola principle, the idea of good rest defence, referring to team-mates behind the ball when their team attacks, ready to defend counter-attacks.

Maresca's City also embody these principles, evident by their 64% possession in their first game against Inter Milan.

On the ball, players in Maresca's set-up play in clearly defined positions rather than moving around the pitch freely. It is obvious the Italian, like Guardiola, is a champion of positional play.

So we have seen Maresca's City leave four or five players – the three defenders and the holding midfielders – behind the ball whilst they attack, ensuring the team maintain a good 'rest defence'.

On the ball, Maresca sets City up in a 3-2-2-3 shape, a shape he used while managing Chelsea.

This rather rigid positional style of play keeps three defenders in the first line, capable of playing with the ball, while being able to cover the width of the pitch defensively.

In front of them, two midfielders help progress the ball, screen the defence, and counter-press quickly if the ball is lost.

In that pairing, we have seen Maresca give licence to one midfielder to contribute to the attack at times – most recently Tijjani Reijnders, linked with a move away, with Mateo Kovacic sitting at the base of midfield.

Ahead of this 3-1 or 3-2 base, wingers are asked to stay high and wide, resisting the urge to leave their position. This is arguably the important part of Maresca's system at City so far.

Nico Gonzalez, speaking after a gruelling game in the heat against K-League All-Stars, provided valuable confirmation.

"I think the idea is clear," he said. "We try to arrive to the wingers. We have a lot of quality in wingers."

In Guardiola's final season, City often used wingers in a narrow fashion, something he explained as being a result of the quality of the players he had available.

But Maresca's system looks to return to using wingers wide – a throwback to the work of Raheem Sterling and Leroy Sane in 2017.

Guardiola's friend and journalist Marti Perarnau spoke to the former City coach about his use of wide wingers during the 2016-17 season.

As noted in Perarnau's book, The Pep Revolution, Guardiola said: "It's a difficult process. You can't just talk to [the wingers] and expect everything to happen.

"My first challenge is to convince [the wingers]. Just stay there on the wing, stay wide. Bide your time, be patient and your moment will come.

"Then, when you do get your chance, think about it, how many opponents am I going to have to get past?

"We've come up with this whole strategy so that you, the winger, only have to dribble past one man and sometimes there will be nobody in your way. On the other hand, if you stop paying attention and drift into the middle, how many will you have to get past? Four!"

Guardiola, of 10 years ago, perfectly describes the logic and strategy behind Maresca's current system, and one that still works.

Across pre-season, Antoine Semenyo, stationed on the flank, was arguably City's standout player, receiving the ball with time and space to run at his full-back. These situations commonly resulted in him arriving close to the box, cutting it back for a forward to tap the ball in, behind the opposition's defence.

For the players behind the winger, the game is simplified into looking to find this repeatable situation.

As heavy as this approach is on dominating through the winger, this does not mean the players infield don't play a valuable role.

If opponents double up on dangerous wingers, the logic is that space will open up inside. This is where attackers comfortable in small spaces, like Phil Foden and Rayan Cherki, may be able to impact games.

Maresca has asked Josko Gvardiol to move from left-back to a left attacking-midfield position when City have the ball, helping form the box shape in midfield.

Both he and Nico O'Reilly have shown an impressive ability to contribute to goals in the final third starting at full-back before arriving into the box. This is a pattern that we are likely to see from City this season.

Out of possession is where we see the biggest changes from Maresca when compared to his time at Chelsea.

At Chelsea, Maresca mainly used a man-to-man press high up the pitch. In pre-season we have seen City defend high up the pitch but in a more zonal fashion – something City did last season.

City's starting shape here has looked like a 4-2-4 before players spring to press certain opponents when the moment is right.

Reflecting on how the game has changed in pre-season, Maresca said: "Usually the team that was defending found the solution by going man-to-man. Now the teams that try to build up are trying to find solutions against man-to-man. I don't know when but there is going to be a bit of change."

And his change in defensive approach appears to be trying to ensure his side are ready for teams who are preparing to play against man-to-man presses more often.

In pre-season, this has been the weakest part of City's system with players, often in midfield or at full-back, having to cover large distances, leaving gaps in their defensive shape.

Like with any defensive approach that involves an element of pressing, this improves with time, as players better understand the press, as well as when physical condition improves.

But this was a part of the game Guardiola tweaked often last season, struggling to land on something he was completely happy with.

There is benefit in Maresca's hire following Guardiola because it provides a sense of familiarity, particularly in the team's identity and their principles.

The 3-2-2-3 shape was the shape City won the treble with. The high and wide wingers, given multiple one-against-one situations per game, and the focus on cut-backs were seen in City's centurion season.

Meanwhile, the use of full-backs moving infield and attacking the box were obvious in City's 2025-26 campaign – as was their 4-2-4 defensive shape.

Maresca's system is its own but interestingly there are references to City's last decade as the club look to begin a new chapter.

title: When do the major European leagues start and what are the big stories?
description: BBC Sport looks at the big stories in Europe heading into the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
The start of the Premier League may still be a week off, but in Europe the new season is already getting under way.

With La Liga kicking off this weekend and Ligue 1, Serie A and the Bundesliga soon to follow, there are plenty of storylines to look forward to this season.

BBC Sport rounds up the best and looks ahead to what should be an enthralling campaign on the continent.

First La Liga match: Alaves v Getafe, Saturday 15 August, 18:30 (BST)

Jose Mourinho returning to Real Madrid 13 years after his first spell as manager ended was a reunion nobody saw coming.

Many expected Real to dominate La Liga and the Champions League when they signed Kylian Mbappe in 2024, and while he has impressed, the team as a whole has not gelled.

Last season Real looked like two teams on the same pitch - a group of four superstar attackers, and a fragile defensive unit left vulnerable to counter-attacks.

New signings Marc Cucurella, Ibrahima Konate, Denzel Dumfries and Bernardo Silva should help shore things up, while Yan Diomande could provide even more excitement in the final third.

Vinicius Junior has also recently agreed a new deal after being linked with Arsenal.

Some suggest a veteran Mourinho has had his day - can he manage the egos of Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius after his previous time in charge at the Bernabeu ended following dressing room disquiet, and does the Special One still possess the tactical acumen to seriously challenge Barcelona?

Hansi Flick's side were not as formidable last season as in 2024-25, but a squad full of Spanish World Cup winners are still favourites to win a third consecutive league title.

Replacing the goals of Robert Lewandowski will not be easy, but reinforcements have arrived in the shape of Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi.

As usual, Atletico Madrid will look to muscle their way into the top two, with Villarreal and Real Betis heading up the best of the rest.

After fighting their way up from the third tier, Malaga will look to avoid the drop with a budget but tightknit squad - they have been under judicial administration since 2020.

There will be tears in Valencia as Los Che play their final campaign at the iconic Mestalla stadium, but who knows if Uefa Conference League runners-up Rayo Vallecano will be able to play any home games at all.

The regional government of Madrid has stripped the club of its license to host matches at its rented Vallecas stadium due to the dilapidated state of the facilities.

La Liga to inspect Celta Vigo's pitch after fungus outbreak

New season, new boss - will Alexander-Arnold be key figure at Real Madrid?

First Serie A matches: Udinese v Como & Inter Milan v Monza, Saturday 22 August, 17:30 (BST)

Inter Milan are fancied to defend their Serie A crown, albeit partly because few teams look equipped to challenge them.

Napoli, AC Milan, Atalanta and Lazio all have new managers, while Juventus and Milan are both under pressure after missing out on the top four last term.

While the absence of Champions League football could aid their title bids, playing Thursday nights in the Europa League could hinder them.

How Ruben Amorim gets on at San Siro will be particularly interesting for Manchester United fans.

Napoli, whose two most recent title defences have fallen disappointingly flat, will hope Max Allegri can rediscover his knack for winning.

Como were the big story of last season, but can Cesc Fabregas' side replicate their league success while navigating a debut Champions League campaign?

They face a race against time to complete improvements at their idyllic lakeside stadium if they are to host European games.

Given the recent struggles of the Italian national team, Fabregas has pledged to try and bring through more young Italian players. Will others follow suit?

Roma did well to finish third last season after a rocky start, and have backed manager Gian Piero Gasperini in the transfer market. Can they kick on and win a first Scudetto since 2001?

Mourners line streets of Milan for legend Baresi's funeral

Defender Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer

First Bundesliga match: Bayern Munich v VfB Stuttgart, Friday 28 August, 19:30 (BST)

The age-old question is as relevant as ever after Vincent Kompany's side cruised to a domestic double last season while playing some truly scintillating football.

Harry Kane is 33 now but is showing no signs of slowing down - the England captain has scored 98 goals in 94 Bundesliga games and has broken countless records.

While questions may be asked of 40-year-old goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and his unconvincing backline, Bayern's devastating firepower of Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Diaz, plus the addition of Morocco international Ismael Saibari, means they should easily outscore their opponents.

Borussia Dortmund, RB Leipzig and Bayer Leverkusen are all capable of launching title challenges, but tend to come unstuck against stubborn mid-table sides.

Elsewhere, fallen giants Schalke 04 are looking to re-establish themselves as a top flight side after three years away. Their promotion heralds the return of one of the fiercest derbies in world football - the Revier derby against Dortmund.

Elversberg were playing in the regionalised fourth tier as recently as 2021-22, but secured promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time in their history to complete a fairytale rise.

With a population of about 13,000, Spiesen-Elversberg will be the smallest town to be represented in the Bundesliga. The odds are stacked against them.

Kane set for talks with Bayern Munich over new deal

Ex-Man City striker Dzeko, 40, pens new Schalke deal

First Ligue 1 match: Marseille v Strasbourg, Friday 21 August, 19:45 (BST)

It is hard to see anything other than Paris St-Germain winning Ligue 1 for the 13th time in 15 seasons, especially off the back of back-to-back Champions League triumphs.

That said, Luis Enrique's side can be got at - last season they lost six league games, two more than in the previous two campaigns combined.

PSG have added attacking midfielder Maghnes Akliouche from Monaco and Aston Villa left-back Lucas Digne to their star-studded squad this summer, but could end up selling wingers Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye amid interest from Liverpool.

Monaco (2016-17) and Lille (2020-21) are the two most recent sides to topple the Parisians, but neither looks equipped to do so again.

Financial difficulties have limited traditional heavyweights Marseille in the transfer market, with more key players set to follow Mason Greenwood out of the club.

Will Still (Auxerre) and Liam Rosenior (Paris FC) are back in the league after ill-fated managerial spells in England, while former Brazil full-back Felipe Luis has been installed as Monaco boss.

Lens were PSG's closest challengers last season, but may need time to bed-in new manager Dino Toppmoller. Lille, who finished third, face a similar situation with Davide Ancelotti.

Strasbourg have been a team on the up in recent years, but after losing manager Rosenior and then Gary O'Neil to the Premier League, face another restart under the relatively inexperienced Hugo Oliveira.

After losing the spine of the team that reached the Uefa Conference League semi-finals last season, the Alsace side have suffered some heavy defeats in pre-season.

Pogba expected to have Monaco contract terminated

Digne completes move to PSG from Aston Villa

Plenty of big names have joined Turkish clubs in recent years, but Mohamed Salah signing for Trabzonspor came as a surprise.

After leaving Liverpool at the end of his contract, Salah decided to join the 2021-22 Super Lig champions rather than one of Turkey's big three - Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas. He'll be remembered as a hero if he can deliver a title at the first time of asking.

In the Netherlands, PSV Eindhoven are looking to win a fourth successive Eredivisie title.

Ajax and Feyenoord are looking to bounce back from disappointing campaigns having since appointed new managers - Spaniard Michel at Ajax and former Netherlands captain Giovanni van Bronckhorst in Rotterdam.

Porto are looking to successfully defend a Primeira Liga title for the first time since 2013, but will surely be challenged by Clasico rivals Benfica, now under the management of Marco Silva.

Sporting CP are looking to reclaim the title after winning it in 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The Eredivisie and Primeira Liga are already under way, while the Turkish Super Lig begins on Friday, 14 August with Galatasaray v Corum (19:30 BST).

title: The main contenders to replace Rodri at Man City
description: As a move for Manchester City midfielder Rodri looks increasingly likely, BBC Sport takes a look at the options to replace him.
fullText:
Enzo Maresca has been in his new job as Manchester City boss just six weeks, but already he may be on the cusp of having to make a tough decision.

With Rodri heavily linked with a move back to his native Spain, Maresca's first challenge may well be to find a replacement for a World Cup-winning captain and Ballon d'Or winner.

Rodri, 30, is in the final year of his contract and City have already rejected a £38.5m bid from Barcelona following interest from Real Madrid.

After helping the Blues win the Treble in 2023 then triumphing at the Euros with Spain a year later, an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed Rodri's dominance somewhat.

But he showed glimpses of his brilliance for City last season before returning to the Rodri of old as he captained Spain to World Cup success in the summer.

His stock is high, and a move from Manchester after seven seasons with the club would leave a huge hole for Maresca to fill.

So who are the leading candidates to step into the Spaniard's boots?

Age: 18 Country: Morocco Club: Lille

Talk of City signing Bouaddi has been rumbling all summer, and the club have reportedly held talks with the Moroccan,, external who would cost an estimated £85m.

Bouaddi is said to be keen on the move.

The teenager impressed at this summer's World Cup after a starring role in Lille's Champions League victory over Real Madrid in 2024 announced him on the big stage.

Bouaddi functions as a deep-lying conductor - much in the same vein as Rodri - and would complement summer signing Elliot Anderson, who is more of a box-to-box midfielder.

Taking into account the loss of Bernardo Silva, it is not just Rodri that City are trying to replace and, with 30 Ligue 1 appearances last season, Bouaddi possesses a level of experience beyond his age.

Age: 25 Country: Argentina Club: Chelsea

City have been heavily linked with Fernandez, and he is currently the favoured option for Maresca, who worked with him at Chelsea.

But the London club are expected to stand firm on their £120m valuation - a hefty sum considering City have already spent £116m on Anderson.

Maresca made Fernandez captain at Chelsea in the absence of Reece James. The Italian clearly sees Fernandez as not only a talented player but also a leader, something City would be shorn of should Rodri move on.

No-one has made more Premier League appearances under Maresca than the Argentine, whose attacking intent and runs into the opposition box are attractive.

Fernandez returned to Chelsea training this week after helping Argentina reach the World Cup final, where he was sent off as they lost to Spain.

And Chelsea have set a deadline of 17:00 BST on Friday for any offers for him as they look to bring an end to uncertainty over his future before the season.

The club are said to be willing to fully reintegrate him into the squad and would continue to regard him as a key player.

Fernandez scored 15 goals and provided seven assists in 54 appearances for Chelsea last season. Of the options in this list, he also comes out on top for successful passes, passes into the box and successful passes into the final third.

Age: 22 Country: England Club: Bournemouth

City have explored a potential move for England international Scott this summer.

The 22-year-old has rejected contract offers from the Cherries amid interest from other Premier League teams, though his current deal does not expire until 2028 and the club have expressed their desire to keep him.

Bournemouth rejected a £64m bid from Chelsea for the midfielder last month and made it clear that any further approaches would not be welcomed. Advances from Arsenal have also been knocked back.

Scott's energy and ball-carrying ability suit Maresca's preferred style of play - with a heavy emphasis on possession - while his passes into the box and ability to win duels make him an appealing option.

Age: 27 Country: Argentina Club: Liverpool

Perhaps the most surprising name to be linked with City is Mac Allister, but the Blues have explored a potential move for him.

The Argentine is into the final two years of his contract at Anfield and has been a consistent presence in the Reds' midfield during his time there, though he struggled for form during a troublesome 2025-26 season.

As a Premier League winner, Mac Allister would bring top-flight experience and be a ready-made candidate to slot into City's midfield.

A versatile player, he can play as a holding midfielder or as a more box-to-box option. As the oldest option on this list, Mac Allister would also offer a wealth of experience.

Should Rodri depart, Maresca's side are somewhat lacking in leaders, with club captain Silva and experienced campaigners John Stones and Nathan Ake also leaving.

Maresca is believed to want a homegrown player in the leadership group, which consists of Rodri, Ruben Dias and Erling Haaland.

Despite his outspoken nature, Haaland does not seem suited to Maresca's demands of a captain on the pitch, which leaves Dias as the front-runner for the armband.

"Erling was one of the first to send a message when I joined the club," said Maresca.

"At Leicester and Chelsea I had a rule that when we scored the captain had to come to the bench, not to celebrate, but for instructions. But if he scores, then he can celebrate.

"If Erling is the captain, we have a problem... can you imagine?"

Phil Foden has captained City during pre-season and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma is a vocal presence on the pitch, while defender Marc Guehi skippered former club Crystal Palace.

title: Will West Ham bounce straight back up?
description: BBC Sport analyses the season ahead for West Ham, who will be playing in the Championship for the first time in 14 years.
fullText:
When Declan Rice hoisted the Europa Conference League trophy aloft in 2023, few would have envisaged that West Ham United would be preparing for life in the Championship just three years later.

A first major trophy for 43 years followed a Europa League semi-final the season before and would be backed up by another European quarter-final in 2024.

The Hammers also finished sixth and seventh in the Premier League in 2021 and 2022.

It was an era for the east London club in which relative success had become the norm.

But things can change quickly in football and for the first time in 14 years, West Ham will be playing outside the top flight.

The Irons are the favourites for an instant return to the Premier League, which they achieved in 2011-12, though the English Football League (EFL) can be an unforgiving environment, even for a club boasting the biggest stadium in Championship history.

And with an ownership tug of war playing out behind the scenes, which way will it go for West Ham in the 2026-27 campaign? BBC Sport takes a look.

This is a path well trodden by other big clubs in English football in recent history.

Newcastle United have dealt with adversity with relative ease on the two occasions they have been relegated to the Championship, in 2010 and 2017, and bounced straight back.

Aston Villa dragged themselves back following relegation in 2016, but it took three years, including a 13th-placed finish in their first season in the second tier followed by a play-off final defeat before eventual promotion.

But Leicester City, Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United fans can all attest to just how quickly the situation can spiral once a team is sucked into the EFL grind.

Leicester were Premier League champions 10 years ago. This season they will be playing in League One, just two years after relegation from the top flight.

Blackburn lifted the title in 1995 and enjoyed several European campaigns along the way.

But Rovers were relegated to the Championship in 2012 - and to League One in 2017. They are yet to get out of the EFL.

Similarly in 2005, Leeds were relegated just four years on from a Champions League semi-final and one year after a UEFA Cup campaign.

It would take 16 years and a journey down to the third tier before Leeds played in the Premier League again.

It was Jarrod Bowen who netted the dramatic last-minute winner for West Ham against Fiorentina on that memorable night of European glory in June 2023 to etch his name into the club's history books.

And Bowen committing his future to the club is perhaps better than any summer signing West Ham could have made.

Bowen has been the club's top goalscorer in four of the past five seasons, netting 76 times in 227 games in all competitions.

He has also provided 53 assists and signalled his intent for the current campaign in Saturday's 3-1 victory over Portsmouth in the EFL Cup, scoring one and setting up another.

An England international, a player of his pedigree could prove invaluable.

"It was a no-brainer for me to be here and the vision is clear," said Bowen after confirming he would stay at the London Stadium. "It's the Premier League."

But the 29-year-old is fully aware of the challenge the Championship provides.

"It's 46 tough games, midweek, Saturday, Tuesday, Friday," Bowen said.

"There's going to be disappointment at times, there's going to be a lot of pressure on us to go and win the league straight away.

"That's our aim, but I'm telling you now, it's not going to be as easy as that."

Manager Nuno Espirito Santo agrees.

"Normally when a team drops to the Championship, you have to be the favourite, mainly because our objective is to go back to the Premier League," the 52-year-old told BBC Radio London.

"We realise how hard it's going to be. We're going to have to be resilient, to keep going.

"Tight schedule, very tough competition, a lot of good teams with the same aspirations as ourselves.

"But we are ready for the challenge."

Retention of key personnel is arguably the most important factor for the Hammers in 2026-27.

Nuno's choice to remain is a luxury not every relegated side always has - Burnley start the season with a new boss, Nicky Hayen, and likewise Wolves with Cesar Peixoto.

Nuno has been there and done it before at this level with Wolves, winning the Championship to gain promotion in 2017-18.

"I look at West Ham as being the team that has kept hold of an incredible manager," ex-Nottingham Forest and Ipswich Town defender Luke Chambers told the BBC's 72+ podcast.

"I think it's a massive coup. It's almost like having an £80m signing coming in. He is top, top level."

There is a proverbial elephant in the room at West Ham though, with an ongoing ownership saga.

Relegation made high-profile player departures inevitable.

Midfielder Mateus Fernandes signed for Tottenham for £85m, winger Crysencio Summerville joined Saudi club Al-Hilal in a deal worth £60m and Freddie Potts, who came through the West Ham academy, has gone to Belgian champions Club Brugge.

Those exits, in theory, should allow West Ham to reinvest that money.

But with a £104.2m loss in their most recent accounts, new Squad Cost Rules (SCR) to comply with and Amanda Staveley's co-ownership struggle, it is not as simple as splashing out every penny of that £150m to overhaul the squad.

The situation is complex and likely to drag on for several months into the new season.

A consortium led by Staveley - the former Newcastle United co-owner - has agreed to buy the Gold family's 25% stake in the club.

But current co-chair Daniel Kretinsky has publicly opposed Staveley's deal, and appears to be working hard to keep her from getting a foot in the door.

Nuno insists funding for transfers is not a problem.

"It's not about the money. We don't have too much time, but what we can't afford is mistakes," Nuno said.

"We have to make it right. To avoid mistakes is crucial this year. The player that comes in the door has to have the same purpose and be identified with the mission we have ahead."

Glyn: Boardroom issues, inevitably, filter down to the pitch. With this wrangling going on, how is it possible to plan? Not many incomings, so far, and the uncertainty surrounding ownership will not aid that process.

Dave: The way this board and its advisors are working, I can see us doing a Luton, which is sadly nothing more than they deserve. I have supported this club for 58 years and I can not remember a worse time.

Andy: Recruitment, as ever, will be the problem, and I predict after a standard very slow start, we'll finish 5th, missing out in the play-off final.

Brendan: If West Ham can't begin to iron out their very obvious off-field problems, they won't have a chance in the Championship.

How will relegated trio fare in the Championship?

Fighting relegation & eyeing promotion? Championship set for six-team play-offs

Despite concerns from some supporters, those working in the game still expect West Ham to challenge at the top.

"I don't think they will be a Leicester," said Bromley manager Andy Woodman.

"They're a little bit more stable than Leicester were. If they can get a few early results and get that fan base on board, it could be massive. I think West Ham will be a force to beat this year."

Former Nottingham Forest striker Lyle Taylor also believes West Ham's home support - with 50,000 season tickets sold - could be crucial.

"If the fans decide 'we're behind the team, we're behind the manager, we're going to push them over the line,' then I can see West Ham winning the Championship at a canter," he said.

West Ham's squad will take on a fresh appearance when they visit Burnley in their first Championship game of the season on Sunday.

Centre-back Axel Disasi has returned to Chelsea and Callum Wilson has joined Brentford, while Fernandes, Summerville and Potts are long gone.

Winger Manor Solomon, who scored 10 goals in 39 Championship games to help Leeds United win promotion in 2024-25, has arrived from Tottenham for £5m.

Ex-Brighton defender Joel Veltman, 34, has also joined, while Mexico international Edson Alvarez has returned from a loan spell with Fenerbahce, as have James Ward-Prowse from Burnley and George Earthy from Bristol City.

There is still time for further additions and West Ham already have the core of a competitive team.

Keeping hold of key starters attracting interest, including defender Konstantinos Mavropanos, will also be essential to an immediate return to the top flight.

"We are going to face the pressure, that's our job," goalkeeper Mads Hermansen told BBC Radio London. "We are West Ham, we are the biggest club in the league and we want to show that we are going straight back up."

Strong words from the Dane, even if promotion is unlikely to be a formality. Nothing ever is in the Championship.

title: 'Same players making the same mistakes' - Howey
description: Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.  The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.  "I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.
fullText:
Newcastle players were making the "same mistakes" in their 3-1 loss to Everton in pre-season on Wednesday, says former Magpies defender Steve Howey.

The Premier League returns next week and Howey believes Matthias Jaissle's side need the time to work on the same issues from last season.

"I was just a little bit disappointed at half-time because it's familiar players - the players that will be making the starting line-up against Liverpool - that are making the same mistakes again," Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle after the match.

"And I'm talking missing chances, even though they might be half-chances and some of them were but some of them were more than half-chances.

"When you've got the ball getting drilled into you, make it stick, but it's bouncing off players, and I'm just thinking we used to see that last season. And I know there's been the World Cup, and you have still got time to work on these things - it's not going to improve straight away, it's going to take time. But it was just annoying because it is the same players making the same mistakes again.

"They'll have a little bit of a breather as such, they'll stretch off and do whatever they have to do, but then go again at the weekend with the two games before getting really ready for the start of the season. Only they'll know individually and collectively if they're ready, but whether they're ready or not, it's coming."
