title: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich's approach work?
description: As Ipswich prepare for their return to the Premier League, BBC Sport look at how they are approaching the transfer market differently.
fullText:
Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.

Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.

Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.

McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.

Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.

But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential.

When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.

This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.

Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.

New boss O'Neil aims to keep Ipswich in top flight

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.

After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.

A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.

At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship.

A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.

Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.

McKenna's 'Championship all-stars' fell well short of safety, finishing second bottom with just 22 points, 16 adrift of 17th-placed Tottenham Hotspur.

But once relegation had been confirmed, the Northern Irishman maintained that recruitment had been in the club's "best long-term interests", a view that has arguably since been vindicated.

Despite spending heavily on transfer fees, Ipswich's £77m wage bill was comfortably the Premier League's lowest in 2024-25. That restraint, coupled with a massive boost to TV income and the quick gain made on Delap's move to Chelsea, enabled the club to post a £4m pre-tax profit for the financial year ending in June 2025.

Hutchinson's sale to Nottingham Forest later that summer provided another windfall but O'Shea, Clarke, Greaves and January 2025 arrival Jaden Philogene stuck around to play crucial roles as Town secured an immediate return to the top flight.

This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.

Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.

The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.

While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly.

"Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."

The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".

Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".

The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.

It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.

The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.

Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.

The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.

With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?

Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived.

Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

title: Royalty, bombers and racing fairytales - Chepstow at 100
description: BBC Sport Wales recalls the major events at the Monmouthshire track that is celebrating its centenary.
fullText:
It came close to closing within months of first opening, was transformed into an RAF base during World War Two and has staged various music concerts, but this month marks a century of horse racing at Chepstow Racecourse.

The track was the brainchild of 10 local dignitaries who put their money together to purchase 370 undulating acres of picturesque Monmouthsire parkland.

Since opening its doors to about 20,000 spectators in August 1926 for its inaugural meeting, Chepstow has welcomed royalty, Wellington bombers and musicians including Tom Jones.

It has also hosted the richest race in Wales - the Welsh Grand National - for more than 70 years.

BBC Sport Wales recalls the major events at the south east Wales venue, where new milestones continue to be set.

Lords Tredegar, Glanely and Queenborough helped pay for the near-two-mile course on what was Piercefield Park.

Lord Harewood's Conca D'Oro won that first race a century ago before the first jumps meeting held a year later.

Financial concerns almost saw the course fail to survive the first 10 years before steadily establishing itself one of only a handful of courses that hosts both flat and jumps action all year round.

Former Welsh jump jockey Alan Johns says the course has wide appeal among riders.

"Unanimously, Chepstow is loved by jockeys," he said.

"It's what we call a big galloping track so it has really long straights, big sweeping bends and generally that means the best horse wins.

"It probably has the the nicest fences in Britain, horses tend to jump very well here.

"The Aintree Grand National, the Gold Cup at Cheltenham and the Welsh Grand National would be in that sort of breath."

Memorable Chepstow moments have included the Welsh Grand National winner that inspired a Hollywood film, a jockey's world record 12 consecutive wins and another home-favourite winner of the Welsh National.

No rider has managed to match the achievements of champion jockey Sir Gordon Richards who, in October 1933, followed victory in Nottingham with six out of six the next day in Chepstow before adding five more a day later at the same meeting. That run of 12 wins remains a world record., external

But perhaps the biggest fairytale was the remarkable return from injury of Dream Alliance, a horse raised on an allotment near Blackwood by Janet Vokes and owned by a syndicate of friends all paying £10 a week.

In 2008, the horse suffered a severed leg tendon, an injury that under many owners might have led to a horse being put down. But the syndicate refused to give up, paying £20,000 for pioneering stem-cell treatment.

Dream Alliance returned to action and repaid their faith as jockey Tom O'Brien rode the then eight-year-old to Welsh Grand National glory in 2009 at odds of 20-1.

The story was perfect for Hollywood, with Dream Horse released in 2021 starring Toni Collette and Damian Lewis.

Since 1949, the highlight of Chepstow's callendar has been the Welsh Grand National, traditionally held during the Christmas festive period.

The race has grown in stature with Bindaree, Corbiere, Earth Summit, Rag Trade and Silver Birch among those to complete the Aintree and Chepstow double.

Meanwhile Burrough Hill Lad, Cool Ground, Master Oats and Native River have proven their pedigree at Chepstow before Cheltenham Gold Cup glory.

One of the most memorable modern occasions came when Welsh-trained Haiti Couleurs won the 2025 edition of the the Welsh Grand National in front of a passionate home crowd.

The horse was trained by Pembrokeshire-based Rebecca Curtis and ridden by champion jockey Sean Bowen.

"As a Welsh jockey or a Welsh person in racing, it's one of the races at the very top of the list to be involved in," added Johns.

Among plans for the future of Chepstow is a three-day jump racing festival which organisers hope will offer an "intimate" alternative to the Cheltenham Festival.

The Welsh Racing Festival was first held last October to launch British National Hunt season.

But for now, racecourse executive director Luke Admans is happy to celebrate the past at a centenary dinner at Chepstow on Thursday.

"I wanted to do something that was going to pay tribute to the 100 years of the racecourse and all the effort it took to get the racecourse open and the work that everyone's done [in that time] to make it such an amazing venue," he said.

"We've got an amazing team. We have a lady who's been working in the annual members area for 53 years and a couple of guys on the grounds team that have been here more than 40 years.

"It's one of them places that I think you come and you fall in love with working here which is amazing and the staff are a tribute to the venue."

title: What are your favourite new kits for the coming season?
description: BBC Sport has rounded up some of the best new kits released by clubs around the world over the summer - vote for your top 10
fullText:
As a new season draws near, football-hungry fans around the country will be tweaking their fantasy teams, making themselves experts on rumoured transfer targets and keeping eyes keenly trained on new kit releases.

It's an exciting time for collectors, whether they're looking for never-before-seen designs, classic shirts reimagined or niche releases from far-flung lands to impress their colleagues at five-a-side.

BBC Sport has rounded up a non-exhaustive list of some of the best kit releases for 2026-27 so far, ordered alphabetically.

Scroll down to the bottom of the page to vote for your top 10.

Marking 20 years since AC Milan's last Champions League title, the Rossoneri's new away shirt is modelled by legendary former player Filippo Inzaghi - who won the trophy twice with the club, including scoring a brace in the 2007 final in Athens to beat Liverpool - and current defender Davide Bartesaghi.

League One side AFC Wimbledon's away kit, in red and yellow, shares the same colour palette as the kit the team wore on the day of their promotion to the top flight for the first time ever on 3 May 1986.

Marking 20 years since the Gunners moved to Emirates Stadium, Arsenal's new home shirt has a bold red base, with white accents.

Mikel Arteta's men kick off their Premier League title defence against promoted side Coventry City on Friday 21 August.

The north London club have reprised their famous yellow for this season's third strip, with a kit reminiscent of away shirts worn by Arsenal players during the late 1980s.

Aston Villa's new home kit is an instant classic. However, the club were warned over sportswashing after revealing Visit Rwanda - the African country's tourist board - as their new front-of-shirt sponsor last month.

Atletico Madrid's new home shirt platforms the Rojiblancos' famous stripes, together with a subtle trident motif - a symbol associated with the club's fans, who gather at Madrid's Neptune Fountain to celebrate victories.

The Blaugrana have adapted their traditional stripes for this year's home kit. Hansi Flick will be aiming for a third successive La Liga title since taking over as manager in May 2024.

Adidas have gone for a retro revival with many of their kits this year and Bayern Munich's away strip sits very much in that vein - simple, clean and with the traditional trefoil logo. Vincent Kompany's team reached the Champions League final last season and have become one of the most exciting teams to watch in Europe.

Blackburn Rovers' new partnership with Umbro has been launched with an absolute stunner of a kit.

After they survived relegation from the Championship last season, manager Tony Mowbray returned to Ewood Park in June for his second spell in charge at the club.

Bournemouth struck a club-record deal with new kit supplier Hummel in May.

German manager Marco Rose will succeed Andoni Iraola at Vitality Stadium this season after the Spaniard departed having led the Cherries to their first ever European qualification.

In a commitment to affordability and sustainability, Brentford announced earlier this month that their new home kit would also be worn during the 2027-28 season.

Brighton's new home kit, with its subtle pinstripes and white neckline, draws heavily on the strip worn by the Seagulls during the 1983 FA Cup final, which they lost 4-0 in a replay against Ron Atkinson's Manchester United.

Celtic's new home shirt celebrates 60 years since the Lisbon Lions defeated Inter Milan to win the European Cup at the Estadio Nacional in Lisbon, with a commemorative badge and inscription inside the neck.

Chelsea's new home kit pays homage to their nineties 'Italian Renaissance', when Gianluca Vialli and Gianfranco Zola helped bring success to the club, including the 1997 FA Cup and 1998 League Cup.

Mexican side Club America's new home shirt is inspired by one worn during the 1998-99 season, with the club's crest blown up across the torso.

Manager Cesc Fabregas has turned Como into a serious outfit and this is a serious kit to match. The Italian side qualified for the Champions League for the first time last season and will be hoping to kick on from there.

Coventry City's new home shirt draws inspiration from the kit worn by players during the 1987 FA Cup final victory over Tottenham Hotspur.

The Sky Blues will return to the Premier League in August for the first time in 25 years after gaining promotion under manager Frank Lampard.

Scottish Championship side Dunfermline Athletic have released a shirt that harks back to the one they wore during the 1994-95 season.

The Toffees' new home shirt draws inspiration from marine flags found around the docks at the Hill Dickinson stadium.

Turkish club Fenerbahce's new away shirt is inspired by the first kit the club ever wore when they were founded in 1907.

Marking the club's centenary, Fiorentina's new home shirt features an embossed pattern inspired by the ornamental frames of Renaissance art found in the city of Florence.

Fulham's away shirt is a reinterpretation of an iconic chequered jersey worn 30 years ago during the 1996-97 season.

In 1996-97, Grimsby Town played in an away kit that was almost identical to one worn by the likes of Roberto Baggio, George Weah and Paolo Maldini at AC Milan. With Lotto returning as the League Two club's kit supplier this season, that design has been revived for a new generation of Mariners fans.

Launching their new partnership with Oxen, Hull City have released a very retro kit for the new campaign, evoking the shirts the Tigers wore during the late seventies.

Sergej Jakirovic's team will return to the Premier League for the first time in a decade this season, kicking off their campaign at home against Manchester United on Saturday 22 August.

Ipswich Town return to the Premier League this season after they were relegated at the end of the 2024-25 campaign.

The Tractor Boys' new home kit takes inspiration from the Sir Bobby Robson and Sir Alf Ramsey stands at Portman Road, with a motif copying the one that runs across the roof of the stadium.

After last season's experimental home kit, the Old Lady have returned to their traditional, thick stripes this year.

Leeds' new away shirt takes the Yorkshire rose from its club badge and repeats that motif across the base of the shirt. Blooming marvellous.

Liverpool's away shirt is inspired by the ticket stubs from European nights during the 1970s and 1980s. It also strongly brings to mind away and third kits worn during a successful period in the club's history during the late 1980s.

Liverpool's home kit for the 2026-27 campaign is a very conscious nod to the Adidas kit the Merseyside club wore between 1989-1991, during which time they won the 1989-90 First Division title under manager Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Lyon's home shirt for the new campaign pays tribute to the city, with Lyon's coat of arms silhouetted against the shirt sponsor and appearing as a subtle pattern across the stripes.

Manchester City's new home kit uses a sky blue gradient, with a print inside the neck, which reads, "Not Your Typical City". Following the departure of Pep Guardiola though, will it be typical City under new manager Enzo Maresca?

Manchester United's new away shirt is inspired by the Red Devils' 1988-90 third kit, which was only worn in three matches. The club have a history of success in blue however, having won both the 1968 European Cup final and 2017 Europa League final wearing blue kits.

Manchester United's new home kit, with its flat-knit striped collar and cuffs, is inspired by Red Devils kits from the late seventies.

To celebrate 150 years since they were founded, Championship club Middlesbrough have released this bold red and gold kit, with a special anniversary club badge displayed front and centre.

Napoli celebrate their founding in 1926 with this special kit in 'centenary blue', featuring a 100-year anniversary logo on the club badge.

Napoli's third kit evokes designs famously worn during the 1986-87 and 1988-90 seasons, when a certain Diego Maradona inspired the club to two Serie A titles.

Newcastle's new home kit uses what's been described as a 'disrupted stripe'. Just don't say it looks like a barcode. The Magpies are entering a new era this season after the shock departure of manager Eddie Howe.

French side Nice have released this classic home shirt and it is, dare we say, rather nice.

Nice's away shirt is another contender for kit of the season with its simple, but effective colour palette, classic fold-over collar and piping down the sleeves.

Nottingham Forest's home shirt is inspired by the mist that rolls in from the River Trent.

Oxford United teamed up with local street artist and lifelong U's supporter Andrew Manson to design this season's kit, along with a bespoke piece of artwork.

The European champions haven't tried to reinvent the wheel with this kit, but it oozes class. Can anyone stop Luis Enrique's side from winning a third successive Champions League trophy?

Primeira Liga champions Porto have released an away kit in gorgeous ruby - inspired by the port produced in the region as well as the River Douro.

Rangers' new home shirt is a classy affair. The Glasgow club will hope to exorcise the disappointment of last season's third-place finish under new manager Derek McInnes.

The stripes are narrower and there are interwoven diagonal lines, but this is still very definitely a Real Betis shirt - one of the most recognisable designs in European football.

Real Madrid have released their new away kit in a gorgeous, deep green, reminiscent of their 2012-13 third kit.

To celebrate their 100-year anniversary, La Liga club Real Oviedo have released a kit worth waiting a century for.

La Liga 2 side Real Valladolid's home shirt uses the club's traditional stripes, with a silhouette showing the Province of Valladolid stitched into the kit.

Sampdoria's home kit will remind fans of a certain vintage of Saturdays and Sundays spent watching David Platt represent the Serie A side on Channel 4's Football Italia.

To celebrate the club's 80-year anniversary, the shirt comes with a subtle anniversary logo embossed across the chest.

Sheffield United's away kit revives a classic style worn by the Blades during the 1975-76 season.

That campaign ended in relegation from the First Division for the Yorkshire club, but it's an iconic design nonetheless.

Ligue 1 side Strasbourg have joined the nineties revival. Their new away kit uses diamond graphics synonymous with Adidas kits from that decade, including the strips worn by the French side themselves between 1994-96.

In one of the more unexpected launches this summer, Sunderland have collaborated with the Elvis Presley estate to release this striking kit in a colourway synonymous with the King's early years in Louisiana.

Elvis' 'Can't Help Falling in Love' has been a matchday anthem for the North East club since the late seventies.

For their new home shirt, the Black Cats have drawn inspiration from the shirt worn by players during the club's first FA Cup victory at Wembley over Preston North End in 1937. A jacquard 'S' in the style of the handles of the FA Cup trophy is repeated across the base of the jersey.

After recording their highest ever WSL points total last season, Spurs are looking towards a bright future with big ambitions in the transfer market. Meanwhile, new manger Roberto de Zerbi is hoping to drag the men's side up from the depths.

To dare is to do and this kit is nothing if not daring.

Serie A club Venezia have released some of the most sought-after kits of recent years and this season's home shirt is sure to be no exception.

Wrexham's new home shirt pays tribute to their stadium, the Racecourse Ground, with a pattern reflecting the old Kop's barriers embossed into the weave of the fabric. The stand was demolished in 2023 to make way for redevelopment.

title: Ex-President Joe Biden's cancer has spread, is very painful, son says
description: Former U.S. President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread beyond his bones and is very painful, his son, Hunter Biden, said in an interview with the BBC.
fullText:
Aug 8 (Reuters) - Former U.S. President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread beyond ‌his bones and is very painful, his ‌son, Hunter Biden, said in an interview with the BBC.

• "The cancer ​has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," Hunter Biden told BBC's "Newsnight," according to video posted online on Friday. "It's very painful and it's very debilitating in ‌many respects."

• A spokesman ⁠for the 83-year-old Democrat declined on Saturday to comment on Hunter Biden's interview.

• ⁠Biden revealed in May 2025, less than four months after he left the White House, that he ​had been ​diagnosed with an "aggressive form" ​of prostate cancer, saying ‌at the time that it had spread to his bones.

• A Biden spokesman said in October he was undergoing radiation treatment and hormone therapy.

• Biden was the oldest person to win the U.S. presidency ‌at the time of his ​election in 2020.

• Biden's physical ​health and mental acuity ​drew scrutiny during his 2021 to ‌2025 presidency.

• Biden attended the ​dedication of ​Barack Obama's presidential library in June in Chicago. Biden served as Obama's vice president from 2009 ​to 2017.

• Biden's ‌presidential memoir is scheduled for release on ​November 17.

title: Goals galore - the wildest scores in EFL Cup history
description: BBC Sport looks at some of the wildest games - and scorelines - the EFL Cup has produced as the competition returns for a new season.
fullText:
Some clubs use the early rounds to give experience to young players, shake off the last of their pre‑season rust and perhaps sneak an early season upset, but that can also result in some staggering scorelines.

From 12‑goal thrillers to 10-0 humiliations and penalty shootouts that threaten to last almost as long as the match itself, the EFL Cup has had it all over the years.

Here's a look at the some of the most wild games the competition has ever produced...

Round one, 13 August 2014, Victoria Road

Let's start off with a bang and talk about the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history.

The tie between Dagenham & Redbridge, then in League Two, and a Brentford side recently promoted to the Championship may not have looked the most interesting on paper, but it certainly delivered a gripping match.

A remarkable match was level at 4-4 after 90 minutes and the goals kept coming in extra-time.

The Daggers took the lead for the first time in the 113th minute and looked set to progress as they led 6-5 late on, before Brentford's Harlee Dean scored in the 117th minute to take the match to penalties.

After Jack Connors and Ashley Chambers missed for Dagenham, skipper Kevin O'Connor stepped up to score the winning spot-kick for Brentford.

Round two, 20 September 2005, Adams Park

Aston Villa manager David O'Leary admitted his side were "on the verge" of being part of a cup shock when they faced Wycombe Wanderers in 2005.

But having trailed the League Two side 3-1 at half-time, Villa responded with seven goals in the second half to secure the win.

Some Villa fans reacted angrily when goals from Nathan Tyson, Roger Johnson and Tommy Mooney put Wycombe in a strong position at the halfway stage.

But goals from Milan Baros and James Milner made it 3-3, before a Craig Easton own goal, two from Gareth Barry and further strikes from Milner and Steven Davis completed an emphatic turnaround.

Second round, second leg, 25 October 1983, Boleyn Ground

We're going back to the days when the early rounds had two legs, the tournament was called the Milk Cup, and the day West Ham United recorded their record win.

There was little warning that an eye‑catching scoreline was coming, given John Lyall's Division One leaders had only edged the first‑leg tie 2-1 at Fourth Division Bury.

But West Ham raced to a 5-0 half‑time lead, with Alvin Martin, Trevor Brooking and Tony Cottee tearing Bury apart.

Cottee completed his hat‑trick before the break and the Hammers were just as ruthless in the second half.

Cottee added his fourth, Alan Devonshire got another, Ray Stewart buried a penalty, and Brooking tapped in late on as West Ham reached double figures.

Fourth round, 30 October 2012, Madejski Stadium

An incredible match, the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history, and it took extra-time to find a winner.

Still without a win in their return to the Premier League, Reading threw away any joy their fans were feeling as they led Arsenal 4-0 by capitulating to lose 7-5.

Arsenal found themselves four down after 35 minutes, but Theo Walcott's goal before half‑time sparked a comeback that dragged the match into extra-time.

Marouane Chamakh put Arsenal in front for the first time on the night with a goal in the first period of extra-time, only for Reading striker Pavel Pogrebnyak to make it 5-5.

But Walcott restored Arsenal's lead before Chamakh completed the scoring.

A remarkable night was further added to by the faintly ridiculous moment when Olivier Giroud and Francis Coquelin threw their shirts into the crowd, thinking the match was over, only to have to awkwardly ask for them back once they realised extra‑time was still to come.

Semi-final first leg, 9 January 2019, Etihad Stadium

Burton Albion's first major semi‑final was somewhat ruined as they were roundly thrashed by Manchester City.

The 3,000 Brewers fans had to battle some M6 chaos just to get there and some might have wished they'd stayed stuck in traffic.

Nigel Clough's side had beaten a mixture of Premier League and Championship sides to get to the last four but were powerless to stop a rampant City side.

Gabriel Jesus scored four, with Kevin de Bruyne, Oleksandr Zinchenko, Phil Foden, Kyle Walker and Riyad Mahrez also scoring against the beleaguered League One side.

After Burton's fairy tale cup run finally ended, Clough said that Pep Guardiola invited him in for a glass of wine and quipped he hoped the Spaniard had "more than a glass."

The second leg finished 1-0 at the Pirelli Stadium, sealing a 10–0 aggregate victory for City.

Second round first leg, 23 September 1986, Anfield

League champions Liverpool showed their class with a 10-goal demolition of Fulham.

Steve McMahon scored four and missed a penalty as the Third Division side were swept aside at Anfield.

Ian Rush and John Wark struck early, Ronnie Whelan added a third, and McMahon scored either side of Wark's second.

He hit the bar from the spot before making it seven, with further goals from Rush, McMahon and Nicol sealing the club's biggest victory in domestic competition.

Liverpool then won the second leg 3-2, advancing 13-2 on aggregate.

Third round, 17 September 2024, Deepdale

Yes, 1-1 isn't the most memorable scoreline, but the third-round tie between Preston North End and Fulham in 2024 makes it into the record books after producing the longest penalty shootout in the competition's history.

A total of 34 spot kicks were taken – 31 of which were successfully converted – as Paul Heckingbottom's men booked their place in round four.

Just when it seemed the shootout may never end, Fulham's Timothy Castagne blazed his spot-kick over the bar and Preston midfielder Ryan Ledson – who scored the game's opener in the 36th minute – fired in the decisive penalty.

The shootout eclipsed the previous record set in 2016 when Derby County beat Carlisle United 14-13 on penalties.

title: BBC NI to remain home of Irish Premiership coverage
description: BBC Sport NI agrees a new three-year broadcast deal with the Irish FA and Northern Ireland Football League to ensure the continuation of extensive free-to-air coverage of international and domestic football across BBC iPlayer, online, radio and TV.
fullText:
BBC Sport NI has agreed a new three-year broadcast deal with the Irish FA and Northern Ireland Football League to ensure the continuation of extensive free-to-air coverage of international and domestic football across BBC iPlayer, online, radio and TV.

The new deal means BBC Sport NI will show 30 live Boyle Sports Premiership streams per season - starting with Friday night's north Belfast derby between Cliftonville and Crusaders - as well as 10 senior Women's Northern Ireland international matches and action from domestic cup competitions.

Finals of the Clearer Water Irish Cup and BetMcLean Cup will be shown live on BBC television and BBC iPlayer, as well as streamed coverage of games in the former competition from the fifth round onwards.

Live coverage of the Irish Premiership will also continue on BBC Radio Ulster and BBC Sounds, while highlights from NIFL and Irish Cup games will be available across BBC platforms.

This follows confirmation that BBC Sport NI will broadcast every Northern Ireland senior men's international until June 2028.

"This new agreement strengthens our longstanding commitment to bringing audiences the very best coverage of the game in Northern Ireland, from national teams to domestic league and cup competitions," said Neil Brittain, the executive editor of BBC Sport NI.

"Through BBC iPlayer, digital platforms, television, radio and BBC Sounds, we will continue to make local football available to the widest possible audience."

Steven Mills, NIFL Chief Operations Officer, said: "We are delighted to extend our contract with BBC Sport NI and sincerely thank them for their continued commitment and significant investment in our game.

"Their coverage has played a major role in raising the profile of the Premiership, increasing its reach and supporting the continued growth of the league."

Colin McKendry, Irish Football Association President said: "We are delighted that the Clearer Water Irish Cup, our flagship domestic cup competition, and Northern Ireland senior women's international matches will continue to be showcased on BBC Sport NI.

"Their coverage has played a significant role in raising their profile reaching new audiences and inspiring more people to engage with football across Northern Ireland.

title: Stanway boosts Thistle promotion bid - watch live on BBC
description: Mark Wilson believes the aim of returning Partick Thistle to the Scottish Premiership was a huge factor in Ben Stanway signing a surprise new contract as Livingston visit in Friday's live BBC Scotland match.
fullText:
Mark Wilson believes the aim of returning Partick Thistle to the Scottish Premiership was a huge factor in midfielder Ben Stanway signing a surprise one-year deal to stay at the club.

The 21-year-old had been widely expected to leave Firhill in the summer after a standout campaign of 12 goals last term.

Thistle narrowly missed out on promotion, losing out to St Mirren in the play-off final.

"He wants to be part of something special here at Thistle," said manager Wilson.

"He's been here since he was 11, so 10 years at the club.

"In his tenth year, if he can get promotion, it would really be the icing on the cake for him."

The academy graduate was linked with moves to various Premiership clubs throughout last season, with Wilson describing his exit as practically a "foregone conclusion" back in January.

But the Thistle boss is delighted with the turn of events.

"His performances were so eye-catching, of course there was going to be interest," said Wilson. "If I'm being truthful, I was resigned to probably losing him.

"But we always kept ourselves in with a chance, by keeping in constant dialogue with him – particularly [assistant manager] Alex Rae. As time progressed that window of opportunity opened a wee bit."

The Glasgow side are at home to fellow promotion hopefuls Livingston on Friday - live in front of the BBC Scotland cameras – after an opening weekend 1-0 victory away to Greenock Morton.

Wilson is hopeful Stanway can further enhance his credentials by helping take Thistle back to the top flight for the first time since 2018.

"He's got a song about him from the fans as well; it's not often you get that," added Wilson.

"He just felt an absolute connection with this club and a drive to help Partick Thistle out of this division.

"That's testament to the lad. He's got a real purpose and determination about him that our young players - and even our experienced ones - can learn from."

title: 39 moves across five countries - football's ultimate journeyman
description: As he prepares to manage in the FA Cup for the first time, Zeph Thomas tells BBC Sport about his extraordinary career path spanning 39 moves in 18 years.
fullText:
"If I didn't get the money I thought I deserved, I'd be off," says Zeph Thomas, as he attempts to explain a career path that has spanned an extraordinary 39 moves in 18 years.

The Bradford-born winger, 36, is one of football's ultimate journeymen.

Rossington Main (five spells), Mickleover Sports (four spells), Frickley Athletic (three spells), Garden City Broncbusters (United States), Montegnee (Belgium), Thunder Bay Chill (Canada).

Thomas' list of former clubs goes on and on.

Cowdenbeath, Boston United, Harrogate Town, Scarborough Athletic, Stafford Rangers, Leek Town.

Ilkeston Town, Matlock Town, Goole, Glossop North End, Stocksbridge Park Steels, Brighouse Town (two spells), Emley, Harrogate Railway Athletic, Sheffield, Shaw Lane, Belper Town, Parkgate, Campion, Eccleshill United, Selby Town and Ossett United.

But could Thomas' life on the move be over?

The former St Kitts & Nevis international has embraced his player-manager role at ninth-tier South Yorkshire club Dearne & District since being appointed in 2024.

After winning the Northern Counties East League First Division last season, the village club based in Goldthorpe, near Barnsley, play their first ever FA Cup match on Saturday when they visit Runcorn Town - one of 219 extra preliminary round ties scheduled to take place.

"We've gone from being in the Doncaster Saturday League in 2021 to playing in the FA Cup," adds Thomas.

"It's massive for the area because they have never seen this team play in the competition."

Where & when? This weekend's FA Cup extra preliminary round fixtures

Thomas' career started at Rotherham United when former Manchester United forward Mark Robins was youth team coach.

He was released in 2008 without making a senior appearance, a decision that did not come as a complete surprise to him.

"I was a bit petulant and naive back then," he says.

"I remember scoring in a reserve game and then the next day we had to come in for recovery runs. At the time, I didn't think I should have been doing any of that.

"If my attitude had been better I would probably have been fine to be honest."

With his dreams of making it big in the full-time game shattered, Thomas embarked on a remarkable journey across non-league football in England, while there were spells at clubs in Kansas, Ontario, Scotland and Belgium.

In 2013-14 alone, he was on the books of Sheffield, Mickleover Sports, Scarborough Athletic, Matlock Town and Goole, while he started 2016-17 back at Mickleover Sports and then went to Shaw Lane, Stafford Rangers, Frickley Athletic... before ending back at Mickleover.

The non-league club where he spent his longest spell was Brighouse Town (second stint) between 2020 and 2023.

While at Stocksbridge Park Steels, he played against Jamie Vardy, then at Halifax Town, before Vardy went on to play for England and win the Premier League with Leicester City in 2015-2016.

In 2013, Thomas almost quit playing after suffering a groin injury. He worked in a call centre in Rotherham and thought about joining the army before being given an opportunity to resume his career at Thunder Bay Chill in Ontario.

Has he kept a record of his numerous destinations?

"Not at all. There's definitely been too many to count," adds Thomas.

"It's been a good experience but it could have been better. I moved up or went sideways for more money.

"But playing in different countries was a great experience and I would encourage all young players to go and experience that if they get a chance.

"I worked under different coaches with different ideas and philosophies."

Zeph Thomas: The unknown local player set to feature on the international stage

From international debut to call centre in five months

After a life spent seemingly on the road, Thomas does not have so far to travel to games these days.

He lives a five-minute walk from Dearne & District's ground, with wife Marie and their two children, Jerome, 11, and Lucia, seven.

Thomas combines his part-time job with Dearne & District, who attracted a crowd of 453 for the home league game with Penistone Church on 28 July, with his role as lead coach for Derby County's Under-12s.

He is still registered to play for the non-league club but these days prefers to coach from the dugout and pass on his experience to players.

"Sometimes I feel a bit of a hypocrite because I used to move clubs for extra money," he says.

"Now I say to my players, 'keep on doing what you're doing because the money will come'."

title: European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage
description: Timetable and BBC coverage times for the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham from 10-16 August.
fullText:
The first European Athletics Championships to be held in Great Britain take place in Birmingham from 10-16 August.

The Championships get under way at Alexander Stadium on Monday, just over a week after the conclusion of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Among the British stars on show are defending champions Keely Hodgkinson and Dina Asher-Smith, local boy Matthew Hudson-Smith, Katarina Johnson-Thompson, Amy Hunt, Georgia Hunter Bell and Jake Wightman.

Sweden's Armand Duplantis, Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen and Greece's Miltiadis Tentoglou are all seeking to win their fourth successive European titles, while Italy's Marcell Jacobs is targeting his third 100m title in a row.

The BBC will bring you comprehensive coverage of the championships on BBC One, BBC Two, BBC iPlayer, Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website, the BBC Sport app and the BBC Sport social media channels including YouTube.

Asher-Smith (100m), Hodgkinson (800m), the women's half marathon team and the women's 4x100m relay squad all won gold as Great Britain came third in the medal table at Rome 2024.

Hosts Italy won 11 golds, and a total of 24 medals, to top the medal table followed by that year's Olympic hosts France with four golds and 16 medals overall.

GB topped the medal table in Brussels in 1950 and Budapest in 1998 before finishing first at Zurich 2014, Berlin 2018 and Munich 2022, with the championships being held every two years since 2010.

There are 50 gold medals to be won at these championships and with home advantage, the British team will be hoping to get back on top of the podium.

Hodgkinson & Asher-Smith in GB squad for Europeans

Sprinter Asher-Smith has won six European golds and two silvers from four championships and could overtake the seven golds of Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic (formerly Perkovic) to become the most successful athlete in the history of the championships.

The 30-year-old could also overtake fellow sprinter Irena Szewinska of Poland as the most-decorated European athlete of all time. Szewinska won a total of 10 medals from 1966-1978.

Of other current athletes, Norwegian star Ingebrigtsen has six golds (no other medals) and Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol has five golds and a bronze from just two championships.

On the men's side, Hudson-Smith has four golds and seven medals in total.

One more medal and he will equal France's Christophe Lamaitre as the championships' most-decorated male athlete of all-time.

A gold medal would also bring him level with Roger Black and Sir Mo Farah as the British men to have won most European titles.

Arguably the most-anticipated event for British fans is Hodgkinson's 800m battle with Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol.

Hodgkinson, 24, sat out the Commonwealth Games and comes into the championships fresh from winning the London Diamond League meeting in July.

However, she faces two tough opponents in her quest for another title.

Swiss star Werro, 22, beat Hodgkinson in June and has twice run faster than the reigning Olympic champion this season, edging closer and closer to the 43-year-old world record of one minute 53.28 seconds.

Broeders-Bol, the 26-year-old world 400m hurdles champion, has moved up to 800m and finished just behind Hodgkinson at London Stadium as she gets up to speed in her new event.

The women's 800m heats take place on Tuesday morning, the semi-finals on Thursday morning and the final at 21:45 on Friday, 14 August.

You can watch live coverage of every session on either BBC One or BBC Two as well as iPlayer, the BBC Sport website and the BBC Sport app.

Radio 5 Live and BBC Sounds will be in Birmingham to bring you daily live commentary, while the BBC Sport website and app will feature live text, reports, analysis, video clips and a medal table.

There will also be coverage on BBC Sport's social media platforms, including YouTube.

Gabby Logan and Jeanette Kwakye will present the BBC TV coverage with Steve Cram, Andrew Cotter, Steve Backley, Colin Jackson and Paula Radcliffe commentating on the action.

London 2012 Olympic champions Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill and Greg Rutherford plus Hodgkinson's coach Jenny Meadows will also provide analysis.

All times BST. Times are subject to late changes.

title: 114 days and counting - how damaging is Alcaraz's wrist injury?
description: BBC Sport analyses Carlos Alcaraz's ongoing absence from tennis and why wrist injuries are so difficult to manage.
fullText:
When Carlos Alcaraz walked off the court at Rod Laver Arena in January, he was on top of the world.

At 22, he had just completed the career Grand Slam, beating all-time great Novak Djokovic in the Australian Open final to claim his seventh major title.

A few months earlier he had decimated his rival Jannik Sinner in the US Open final in what was one of most the impressive performances of his illustrious career to date.

But the Spaniard has now missed the French Open and Wimbledon, going 114 days without playing a competitive match due to a wrist injury he suffered in April.

After returning to training, he has now withdrawn from the upcoming Cincinnati Open, and with the US Open less than a month away, Alcaraz's ability to defend his title is in serious doubt.

So, why exactly is Alcaraz's injury proving so troublesome, and how problematic can wrist issues be for tennis players in the long run?

Alcaraz has been suffering from tenosynovitis - a painful inflammation of the fluid-filled sheath that surrounds the tendon on the inside of the wrist.

Tenosynovitis is typically caused by repetitive movements like gripping and swinging a tennis racket, and can lead to swelling and ongoing tenderness.

Minor cases can take weeks to recover, mostly managed by rest, but more severe issues can require significant physiotherapy and potentially even surgery, with recovery taking up to a year.

Alcaraz has not undergone surgery, but his latest withdrawal will take him to over four months out injured, and for a portion of that he was unable to use a racquet at all.

Wrist injuries are particularly worrisome for tennis players. The joint plays a key role in every contact between the racquet and ball - the way the wrist rolls through a shot helps generate power, and its dexterity is vital for delicate touches like drop shots, which are a key part of Alcaraz's all-court game.

The lack of muscle surrounding the bones and tendons in the wrists also makes rebuilding strength difficult, meaning the length of absences can be difficult to predict.

"They're much tougher injuries," 1996 Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek told Tennis365.

"It's really difficult to reset when you start playing again [after this type injury]. You need to go step by step.

"It's not as clear-cut as tearing the ligaments in your ankle, which [you know takes] three or four months and then you can play again."

As tennis has become quicker, with the majority of players on both tours hitting hard from the baseline and using a double-handed backhand, the ability to generate power and top-spin has become even more important, increasing the strain on players' wrists.

Grand Slam winners Dominic Thiem and Juan Martin del Potro both suffered recurring wrist injuries throughout their careers.

"Wrist injuries are becoming more significant in the game," says James Ross, a physiotherapist who works with players at Grand Slams and other tournaments.

"A big factor is technological improvements - racquets and strings are better, so the ball is coming at you with more force and you've got to be able to absorb that.

"Tennis players also have a more gruelling schedule than ever before, putting more strain on the joints, and the balls are inconsistent between tournaments - changes like that mean the body has to adapt and that presents an injury risk."

Alcaraz won his last match against a qualifier in the opening round of the Barcelona Open, but was in visible discomfort and withdrew before his next match.

A competitive return is still a few weeks off at least, however, meaning he will at best be carrying almost five months' worth of rust into the US Open if he plays.

But with wrist injuries in tennis, waiting longer can help prevent the problem recurring.

"The biggest risk of injury is a previous injury - if you have had it once, you are more likely to have it in the future," Ross adds.

"If a player can get back over a period of a few months and they don't have a reoccurrence, generally they will be OK.

"But some things can become chronic and the pressure of the sport to come back, earn money by playing, and keep your ranking points, is a risk."

One of the key challenges of a wrist injury is psychological - once a player has suffered a painful injury in the joint that controls so much of their technique, it can be difficult to fully trust it again.

"Wrists aren't easy", said Sir Andy Murray, having suffered injuries in both wrists in his early 20s.

"When the ball is low you know you really have to use your wrist to get the ball up and down, or when the ball is coming fast and quite high you need to use your wrist a lot to bring the ball down.

"It's difficult when you try to come back [from a wrist injury], because the pain that you feel when you initially hurt it, mentally it's very difficult to let go of."

Before his injury, Alcaraz had been performing at an extremely impressive average of two Grand Slam titles per year. Continuing at that pace would have him level with Novak Djokovic's record of 24 by 2034, when he will be only 31.

Alcaraz will hope to return to top form as soon as he is back on court, but reaching the same level of performance following a wrist injury isn't easy.

"The wrist doesn't get great blood supply and it doesn't heal very quickly," says Ross. "It takes real time to build strength in it and the management is very complex.

"Restoring confidence is down to how rehab goes - you can feel amazing and then get a setback, and it's how you deal with that.

"We also treat injuries as windows of opportunity - you might not be able to hit a tennis ball right now, but let's work on your cardiovascular fitness, work on the core and lower body, or see how you mentally decompress and cope with having a holiday.

"You really have to keep the player motivated."

title: Ex-Brazil forward Pato's consortium to take over Northampton
description: Former AC Milan and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato is a member of a consortium which is set to buy a majority stake in League Two club Northampton Town, BBC Sport understands.
fullText:
A consortium including former AC Milan, Chelsea and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato is set to buy a majority stake in League Two club Northampton Town, BBC Sport understands.

Sports Alpha Capital was in discussions about taking over Colchester United earlier this year but decided to pull out of a potential deal following initial talks.

It is understood Pato is involved with the consortium but is not fronting it.

The 36-year-old retired from playing last year. He is best known for his five-and-a-half-year spell at AC Milan where he scored 63 goals in 150 matches and won the Serie A title in the 2010-11 season.

He spent the second half of the 2015-16 season on loan at Chelsea from Corinthians and scored on his debut from the penalty spot in a 4-0 win at Aston Villa.

The news comes after Northampton chairman Kelvin Thomas confirmed last month that a "well-funded" group's proposed investment had been "pretty much agreed".

The Cobblers suffered relegation to the fourth tier last season, finishing bottom of the League One table.

In April, the club announced a pre-tax loss just short of £3m with Thomas previously saying that the proposed investment would make the club debt-free.

Northampton appointed Chris Hogg as their manager in May and have so far brought in seven new players in the transfer window, including striker Matty Warhurst from Manchester City and midfielder Connor Lemonheigh-Evans from MK Dons.

Brighton will face CFR Cluj (Romania) or Tromso (Norway) in the key fixture. fullText:
On the latest Albion Unlimited podcast, BBC Radio Sussex's Johnny Cantor is joined by former Brighton forward Warren Aspinall as they discuss the Seagulls' possible opponents in the Conference League play-off tie.

Brighton will face CFR Cluj (Romania) or Tromso (Norway) in the key fixture.

Cluj and Tromso are yet to face each other in their two-legged tie, but Cantor believes Tromso could pose a "potential banana skin" for Fabian Hurzeler's side.

"They are placed third in the Norwegian season, which is deep into the campaign as they play across the summer," said Cantor.

In Tromso's Norwegian Eliteserien campaign, they have lost two out of 16 possible games.

In the Romanian SuperLiga, Cluj are also in fourth position, but they have only played three games in the 2026-27 campaign.

Cluj and Tromso's second leg tie will be played on 13 August, with the winner facing Brighton in a two-legged tie on 20 and 27 August, with the Seagulls at home for the second leg.

title: Trump files emergency motion to block BBC from getting financial details about business empire
description: President Trump’s attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust. The British broadcaster received approval from a judge lat...
fullText:
President Trump's attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust.

The British broadcaster received approval from a judge late last month to probe the president's financial documents after Trump claimed he experienced losses due to an episode of the company's "Panorama" series titled "Trump: A Second Chance?"

In the footage, the BBC strung together three separate portions of a speech from Trump to make it look as if he encouraged a violent attack on the Capitol.

"The BBC's improperly broad subpoena demands the Trust's confidential tax, ownership, and financial records for approximately 400 entities," Trump's attorney Alejandro Brito wrote in the legal filing.

"Once the Trust were to begin handing those records over to the BBC, that disclosure could not be undone, and the Trust's pending objections could not restore what the BBC will already have seen," Brito added.

If the emergency motion is not approved, the BBC would be granted insight on Trump's crypto and stock profit, as well as business transactions from at least 400 entities and companies tied to his personal assets managed by family.

Last month, Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett granted the BBC's subpoena to review documents from the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust dating to Jan. 1, 2023.

Her approval requires that the trust start producing documents by Thursday.

"Against the Trust's irreversible injury, the BBC cannot point to any injury, only to brief delay, which does not constitute harm. Fact discovery remains open for months, and the BBC has never explained why it needed a non-party's complete financial records within ten days or how a short stay would impair its defense," Brito wrote.

The BBC has apologized for the documentary edit but has strongly rebuked Trump's push for a payout and attempted to dismiss the lawsuit against the company, arguing U.S. courts hold no legal jurisdiction over the foreign corporation.

The president has refused to back down and recently requested that District Judge Roy Altman allow him to alter the lawsuit in a manner that would shield his financial documents from being reviewed by the British broadcaster.

title: Players who turned World Cup heroics into big transfers
description: BBC Sport looks back at some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned a big transfer.
fullText:
The World Cup is football's biggest stage, filled with goals, drama and unforgettable moments - but it can also prove to be the ultimate shop window.

World Cup heroics have transformed players' lives in the past, and Vozinha's recent move to Chilean side Colo-Colo after an impressive tournament with Cape Verde is the latest reminder that the competition still has the power to change careers.

At the age of 40, the goalkeeper's journey from the Portuguese second division to Chile's biggest club may be unique, but he is not the first to get a big move after starring on the global stage.

Here are some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned them a big move.

Similar to Vozinha, Marc-Vivien Foe was an unknown name before the 1994 World Cup.

Despite Cameroon's disappointing World Cup campaign in the USA, compared to their historic run in 1990, Foe emerged as one of the team's best performers during his debut tournament.

A standout game against Brazil caught attention, which then led to a free transfer from Cameroon's Canon Yaounde to French side Lens.

Foe spent four years at Lens and helped them achieve their first league title in the 1997-98 season.

He also played for West Ham United, Manchester City and Lyon, where he won the French League Cup and Lyon's first Ligue 1 title in 2002.

Foe tragically passed away in June 2003 after he collapsed during a Confederations Cup semi-final against Colombia.

Gilberto Silva's first appearance at a World Cup came in 2002, when the tournament was hosted in South Korea and Japan.

The 25-year-old, who played in Brazil's top division for Atletico Miniero, returned home as a World Cup winner who played every minute of every game for Luiz Felipe Scolari's team.

Silva was only brought into the starting XI because Brazil captain Emerson was ruled out by injury.

But, after playing a key role in Brazil's triumph, the midfielder earned a move to Premier League champions Arsenal.

Nicknamed 'The Invisible Wall', the defensive midfielder joined the Gunners from Atletico Mineiro for about £4.5m.

During his six years in north London, Silva won two FA Cups and played a key role in the famous 2003-04 Invincibles side that went unbeaten to claim the Premier League title.

At the age of 22, Javier Mascherano announced himself on the global stage at the 2006 World Cup, where he helped Argentina reach the quarter-finals.

His performances for both his club back in Brazil and at the World Cup drew the attention of European clubs.

Mascherano initially expressed his desire to remain at Corinthians and help the club in their relegation battle.

However, he soon made the move to West Ham United in the summer of 2006 alongside his Argentina team-mate Carlos Tevez, who also impressed at the World Cup in Germany.

Mascherano had a brief spell with the Hammers until the beginning of 2007, leaving to join Liverpool where he featured in their 2007 Champions League final defeat by AC Milan.

Mascherano then played for Barcelona from 2010, winning the Champions League twice and being part of squads that won La Liga on five occasions.

At the age of just 21, Mesut Ozil emerged as one of the world's most exciting young players after he helped Germany finish third at the 2010 World Cup.

After registering four goals and four assists in seven games, Ozil was able to show off his quality and prove he was a standout performer.

Big clubs took note, and by August 2010, Ozil switched Werder Bremen for Real Madrid, for a fee of about 15m euros (£12.4m).

Copa del Rey, La Liga and Spanish Super Cup titles were to follow during his three year stay in Madrid, before becoming Arsenal's record signing for £42.4m in 2013.

James Rodriguez became one of the stars of the 2014 World Cup, scoring six goals for Colombia and winning the Golden Boot after a memorable run to the quarter-finals.

His excellent performances, including his famous volley against Uruguay, earned him a spot in Fifa's team of the tournament.

The volley against Uruguay was later voted as the best goal in the tournament by more than four million people on Fifa's website and won the Fifa Puskas Award for the best goal of the year.

Real Madrid decided to sign Rodriguez from Monaco for about 75m euros (£71m) after the tournament - a move that led to him winning multiple trophies with Los Blancos, including two Champions Leagues.

Well, you knew this one was coming.

Vozinha became a cult hero when Cape Verde claimed their first World Cup point against Spain in the group stage and his social media fame has exploded from 50,000 Instagram followers to nearly 30 million.

After helping his team reach the knockout stages, taking finalists Argentina to extra time in the last 32, Vozinha was named in Fifa's team of the tournament and even had a newly discovered species of sea slug named after him.

Vozinha's career has taken him to Slovakia, Angola, Moldova, Cyprus and, until recently, Portuguese second division side Chaves, but he has always believed himself to be a "big club player".

Joining Colo Colo, the most successful team in the Primera Division (34 titles) and Copa Chile (14), is his career "highlight".

title: Lynch exit 'pretty much a snap decision' - O'Doherty
description: Derry City chairman Philip O'Doherty tells BBC Sport NI he thought "it was time to make a change" following news of the departure of manager Tiernan Lynch.
fullText:
Derry City chairman Philip O'Doherty has said that the decision to part ways with manager Tiernan Lynch was one that had only been finally arrived at quite quickly.

The Brandywell club announced the departure of Lynch on Wednesday after a disappointing season to date.

The Candystripes sit sixth in the Premier Division table and have won just one of their past seven games.

The former Larne double title winning boss had been manager of Derry since November 2024 and guided them to a second place finish in the league last season, plus qualification for European competition.

O'Doherty told BBC Sport NI that it was "pretty much a snap decision" to part company with Lynch, with it only being finalised on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.

"He [Lynch] had a really good season last year, this year hasn't been up to expectations and has been a disappointment," O'Doherty told BBC Sport NI.

"We've assembled a reasonably good squad we think, and it's getting better with the arrival of Mark Connolly in a director of football role, but I just thought if we were going to make a change now was the right time to do it.

"We've got all to fight for in terms of European spaces and we're still in the cup."

Pressure had been building on Lynch in recent months in light of poor results, with some supporters vocal in calling for a change.

"I don't follow social media and I don't follow a lot of the football pundits either. I look at what's happening on the field and speak to my fellow directors and we make a decision, and we thought it was time," explained the Derry chairman.

"The players weren't expecting it and were probably thinking we will fight through the rest of the season but by and large they understand it.

"He [Tiernan] was disappointed but we shook hands and I wished him the best of luck."

Former club captain and recently appointed director of football Connolly has been named interim manager at the club.

"He [Connolly] knows the squad of players, he lives in Derry, which is very important. Mark was part of the team, he was the captain of the team that got second place last year and he came in as director of football," added O'Doherty.

"Mark would have a lot of respect from those players. Bringing anybody new in was probably going to be difficult anyway.

"I think Mark fits the bill. He's a young manager and I think it will take a little bit of help from the senior players in particular. Michael Duffy is the captain but we will probably need four or five captains because he lacks experience in managing.

"But he has shown all the right qualities so far and he's certainly a man motivator. I just think it's a challenge that he'll rise to and he certainly made himself available once the question was asked."

Club captain Michael Duffy said the players were told the news of Lynch's departure after training and described it as "a difficult day".

"You don't like to see anyone losing their job but it is what it is. As players we move on and try and get three points on Friday. We know we haven't been good enough this year.

"I played with Mark and he's a real leader. He knows football, he knows this group and he knows a lot of the players."

Derry are at home to Sligo Rovers in their next league fixture on Friday night, a game which will be streamed live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website.

"We need to go and play with confidence and build on what we've been doing the past few weeks.

"We need to finish strongly, climb up that table and try to catch that European spot and try to win that cup," Duffy added.

title: How Buttler became T20 cricket's run-scoring GOAT
description: BBC Sport explores how Jos Buttler became the highest run-getter in men's T20 cricket.
fullText:
He did it with a six, of course.

Jos Buttler thrashed Marco Jansen's ball over square leg and on to the balcony of the hotel behind the stand at Old Trafford.

That shot helped the England white-ball great move to 14,833 runs in T20 cricket, surpassing Kieron Pollard's mark of 14,803 to become the highest run-scorer in the format's history.

The Manchester Super Giants number three went on to make 51 from 20 balls, another superb innings in a remarkable 522-match career in the sport's shortest format.

The 35-year-old is in a sparkling run of form in T20s, making 50+ scores in three of his last four Hundred matches - which count towards T20 stats - and hammering a 64-ball 131 in his most recent international outing, a victory over India at Southampton last month.

BBC Sport takes a look at the statistics that put the former England white-ball captain among the greats of the T20 game, and the reasons behind his remarkable longevity.

The race, whether stated or not, has been on since 2022.

That was when Chris Gayle, the charismatic West Indies opener who blazed a trail in the shortest format, played his last professional game, setting a mark of 14,562 runs in T20 cricket.

Buttler was always one of the leading candidates to take the record down.

However, it was another West Indian in T20 journeyman Pollard, 39, who beat him to it, passing Gayle's total in June and extending the record to 14,803 over the course of the Major League Cricket season.

Pollard had the advantage as the leading appearance maker in the format with 741 - 139 more than Sunil Narine in second place.

Buttler sits ninth on that list with 522 appearances and while he is England's highest T20 appearance maker with 160 caps, he doesn't hold the record for most appearances in the format by an Englishman.

That goes to Alex Hales, who has made 528 appearances and was another candidate to break the record - he has 14,429 runs to his name and sits fourth in the all-time list.

Buttler's total includes 1,192 runs scored in 31 matches in The Hundred, with cricket statisticians including data from the competition in T20 records.

It all started in Hyderabad, curiously enough.

Playing in the short-lived Champions League Twenty20 in 2009, Somerset debutant Buttler, who had recently turned 19, emerged at number nine against New South Wales.

A single driven down the ground off Moises Henriques was the first of six runs that day, finishing unbeaten as his side closed on 111 and then lost the match within 12 overs.

When he made his England debut, almost two years later in Manchester, he wasn't called upon to bat as the home side beat India. Indeed, he didn't bat in three of his first four T20I appearances.

Buttler's first taste of life in international cricket was as a lower-order finisher, and his first runs for England in that India series were 13 from number seven.

He started slowly, with an unbeaten 32 against South Africa - his one score higher than 15 in his first 11 innings at international level.

However, former England team-mate Dawid Malan said Buttler's qualities were always evident.

"He started young [he was 20 when he made his England debut]. He always had the scoops and power and he's developed with the modern game," said Malan.

"He's never been left behind and he's almost been at the forefront of pushing the modern game and what players can do."

Buttler's first half-century for England came against New Zealand in 2013, though it took until the 2021 T20 World Cup for his first ton - against Sri Lanka in Sharjah, off 67 balls.

While Buttler has been remarkably consistent in the format - he has averaged fewer than 30 in just one of the past 12 calendar years (2017) - he has really kicked on since 2021, a period which has brought all nine of his T20 tons.

Having emerged as a late-order hitter, his run-scoring became even more prolific when he moved up the order to open the batting for his respective teams.

His record in the powerplay is superb, with an average of 43 in the first six overs of the innings and, of all the English batters to have more than 1,000 powerplay runs in the format, only two better Buttler's average, albeit having played considerably less cricket (Tom Westley and Kevin Pietersen).

And if he's still around during the death overs, Buttler is even more destructive - striking at 184 between overs 16 and 20 compared to 143 at the top of the innings.

It is all based around some very simple principles.

"Jos Buttler's whole philosophy is to hit the ball on the off side," said Malan.

"When you speak to him about batting he is very big on looking off side and, at the death in particular, he's always looking to hit the sightscreen flat. That is weird because generally players are trying to hit the ball high and out of the ground.

"But by doing that [looking to hit the sightscreen flat] he is pushing his left hip at the bowler. He has two things he believes in; hitting the sightscreen and doing that. He gets himself into positions where he's so strong with his base that he can find the ball with his hands."

Ex-England paceman Steven Finn pointed to Buttler's wristy style of play as he added: "The first time I bowled at him in the nets, the ball just made a different sound of his bat.

"The way he turns his wrists and hockey slaps it when he hits a cover drive or when he hits a six down the ground, he's got such strong wrists which I think makes him a bit different to other batters who are more classical with the way they hit the ball."

It is a technique honed in all forms of cricket at the highest level.

"One of the things that people forget is Jos Buttler played 57 Tests for England," said Malan. "He learned his batsmanship through that and learned how to build an innings and how to win games of cricket.

"That education, mixed with his power, means he's able to transfer that to his white-ball cricket."

Perhaps Buttler's greatest strength is his lack of weakness against any particular form of bowling.

Against seam from either hand and versus off-break and slow left-arm spin, the difference in his average is within a margin of a run, sitting between 37 and 38.

Only against leg-break bowling does his average tail off a little, but only to a still respectable 31.31, while he is prolific against the uncommon left-arm unorthodox spin, averaging 48.20.

His boundary ball percentage is marginally better against seam, sitting in the low 20s as opposed to the mid-teens against spin.

His strike-rate is best against the right-arm seamers, against whom he has scored almost 50% of his runs - reflective of the type of bowlers he faces in the powerplay.

Buttler is particularly dismissive of the short ball - averaging 74 against it since 2021 - while of players to have more than 500 runs in the same period, only Pakistan's Mohammad Rizwan averages more against short-pitched bowling.

It's quite staggering that fellow white-ball legends Trent Boult, Matt Henry and Sam Curran have never dismissed Buttler in T20 cricket and only two men have got the better of him more than five times - India duo Bhuvneshwar Kumar and Varun Chakaravarthy.

Afghanistan's Rashid Khan has the best strike-rate against Buttler - removing him six times in just 82 deliveries.

"He's captained and played all around the world and he's been a marquee player," said Malan.

"When you are the marquee player in the team, you get paid the most and the expectation from the owners, captains, coaches and team-mates is that you're going to go out and score runs every single time - and the pressure that comes with that is immense.

"His whole life, he's been able to deal with pressure. That just makes it all the more remarkable what he's done."

Buttler turns 36 on 8 September, and will be 38 by the time the next edition of the T20 World Cup arrives in late 2028.

Of the ICC full members, only Afghanistan carried a player of that age in the 2026 competition, but Buttler has shown few signs of decline and is likely to be part of England's party travelling to Australia and New Zealand.

He struggled in the World Cup earlier this year, averaging 10.87 from eight matches, but with the tournament returning to the grounds where Buttler led his country to victory in 2022, don't count against him lifting the trophy for a second time.

title: Ex-England prop Marler to become BBC's first celebrity Gladiator
description: The former rugby star will be known as Mauler when the fourth series airs in 2027, the BBC confirmed.
fullText:
Former rugby star Joe Marler is to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator on the BBC's popular entertainment series.

The 36-year-old, who also took part in the first series of Celebrity Traitors, will be known as Mauler and face contenders when the fourth series of Gladiators begins in 2027.

"Mauler will see you now," Marler said in a video posted on Instagram, external announcing the news, recorded in the Gladiators dressing room.

The BBC said Marler will make his debut with a series of "special appearances packed with power, personality and plenty of surprises".

Filming for the fourth series is currently under way in Sheffield, the BBC confirmed in a statement.

"Known for his uncompromising style of play and larger-than-life sense of humour, Joe has built a reputation as one of the UK's most entertaining sporting personalities," the corporation said.

"Now, he's taking on an entirely new challenge as he joins the ranks of the Gladiators, bringing his trademark physicality and competitive spirit to one of television's toughest arenas."

The former England rugby international star, who is from Heathfield, Sussex, will join fellow Gladiators such as Nitro, Viper, Diamond and Sabre in battle when the show returns next year.

Gladiators was a hugely successful show on ITV in the 1990s, and saw members of the public take on a group of elite athletes who each had their own on-screen persona.

Olympic swimmer Sharron Davies, who like Marler was already known as a famous sports personality, joined that iteration of the show in 1995 as the character Amazon.

The format was revived by Sky for two series in 2008, before the current iteration launched in 2024, quickly becoming a hit for BBC One.

A celebrity spin-off is separately in the works, featuring contestants including presenter AJ Odudu, comedian Sara Pascoe, podcaster Chris Ramsey and social media star George Clarke.
