title: Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?
description: BBC Sport explores why Fifa president Gianni Infantino feels powerful enough to sell off stakes in the World Cup - and what the consequences could be.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino is billing it as the democratisation of football.

But Fifa's announcement that it aims to sell off stakes in its football competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors via associates of US President Donald Trump has been met with incredulity and rage from fans, politicians and regional governing bodies.

The big selling point, according to Infantino, is $40m (£30m) in funding given to all Fifa countries to "develop the game" once the deal is finalised.

The Swiss has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

This is the boldest move Infantino, an administrator who views himself as a world leader on par with presidents and prime ministers, has made in the decade since he became Fifa president.

If Fifa pushes the plan through, he will have consolidated his power for the long-term future and made investors wealthy along the way.

So why exactly does Infantino feel powerful enough to enact something so controversial, and what could the consequences be?

Infantino has enough support to suggest the plan is more likely to go ahead than not.

Since being elected Fifa president in 2016, Infantino has earned long-standing, widespread backing from many countries in Africa, Asia, and the Americas, which have gained financially from various policies he has managed.

They include the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams, the growth in commercial and broadcast revenue Fifa has overseen, and a programme which allocates millions in funding directly to member countries every year.

That gives him a base of support which constitutes more than half of Fifa's 211 members.

Fifa votes require a simple majority - if more than half vote in favour, Infantino's plan will come into effect.

The proposal will appeal to many nations, particularly those lower down the football food chain, for whom a £15m windfall would be more than they would ordinarily make over several years.

The level of backing Infantino enjoys appears to have emboldened his approach to the presidency. Decisions such as the introduction of hydration breaks and a musical half-time show to the World Cup were taken by his administration without a vote of members, and would have been deemed unthinkable when he took charge a decade ago.

And his close relationship with Trump is key too.

The investment fund Fifa is dealing with - Thrive Capital - is led by Josh Kushner, the brother-in-law of Trump's daughter Ivanka.

Fifa says Greg Maffei, the American former president of Formula 1 owner Liberty Media who has donated to Trump's political campaigns in the past, is acting as a "key commercial advisor".

The proposal follows years of Infantino making overt attempts to deepen his and Fifa's ties with Trump.

He created a Peace Prize and awarded it to Trump. He opened a Fifa office in Trump Tower, New York. He allowed the Club World Cup trophy to be kept in the Oval Office at the White House. He laughed along during Trump's inauguration speech in which he threatened World Cup co-hosts Canada and Mexico.

And last week, Infantino heavily mimicked Trump's language when he released a statement describing those who criticised aspects of the organisation of the World Cup as "so consumed by hate and criticism".

Working with Trump associates on the plan allows Infantino to harness the power of the bond he has cultivated with the world's most powerful person, with the promise of a mutually beneficial outcome.

Fifa has engaged in discussions about the potential sell-off unilaterally, generating anger among nations and regions who feel it was done behind their backs.

But while there is a significant element of risk attached to this move, the chances of Infantino being brought down by it are slim, given how strong support is for him elsewhere.

Fifa would receive a huge influx of cash in one go if the plan is approved, and the proportion earmarked for national federations would be made available from 1 January 2027, according to a letter sent to each country by Infantino.

He added: "The decision whether or not to proceed with this proposal belongs entirely to you.

"In exchange, all that is required is your trust - everything else remains the same."

The appeal is clear - vote to help make us richer and we'll make you richer too.

But each World Cup makes significantly more money than the last - it will probably be worth far 

If Fifa sells stakes now, then the private investors will share in the rewards of that growth in the coming years, rather than Fifa and football doing so alone.

And ultimately, Fifa is a non-profit organisation under Swiss law, meaning its ultimate goal is - theoretically, at least - the long-term wellbeing of football rather than making a profit.

The big winners from the plan, then, would arguably be some of the smaller football nations, the private investors, and Infantino.

"What we know so far about how some national federations spend their money raises a lot of doubts about whether the money reaches the levels of football which Fifa promises," says Miguel Maduro, a former chairman of Fifa's governance committee.

Maduro claims he quit that role after 10 months because Infantino and Fifa's wider leadership disagreed with how the committee was operating.

"Fifa works as a political cartel - it is fed and supported on a system of patronage, that works through the money Fifa distributes to national federations. There have been cases of corruption," he added.

"There is a very high likelihood that this [proposal] will be approved.

"It is a form of legalised bribe."

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa for comment about Maduro's assessment.

Private equity investment has already transformed sports in the USA.

Rules have been changed in baseball, basketball, American football and ice hockey to allow for more minority investments in the past decade, causing team values to skyrocket.

And La Liga and Ligue 1 have already sold portions of their operations to private equity firm CVC Capital Partners in exchange for an immediate influx of money.

Infantino is hopping on a trend in sports economics rather than trying out something entirely new, but stands to further entrench his own power if he succeeds.

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

Infantino's proposal has deepened his ongoing conflict with European governing body Uefa - the most powerful and wealthy regional organiser.

Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin boycotted the World Cup final in protest against Fifa's decision to overturn USA striker Folarin Balogun's suspension after an intervention from Trump.

That followed a series of Uefa announcements making clear it would not follow Fifa policy on controversial issues including dynamic ticket pricing and hydration breaks.

One of the cornerstones of the division between the two is that Fifa's revamped and expanded Club World Cup has become a clear, direct threat to Uefa's Champions League.

Previously Uefa was the only organisation which ran an international club football competition featuring the best players, watched by billions around the world and generating significant profits.

Last summer Fifa muscled in on that elite club football territory, adding teams from other continents to the mix.

Some national federations have expressed anger that they found out about the plans only when Fifa made them public, but crucially, many of the statements released so far have not explicitly condemned the concept of the sell-off itself.

That said, BBC Sport understands many Uefa members are angry about the plan and that a meeting is set to be convened for them to discuss a response.

On Tuesday Uefa said Fifa's plan is "to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends".

Some reports indicate a threat by European nations to boycott the World Cup could be possible. The theory is that a World Cup without European countries would severely compromise the tournament's value to Fifa.

But the chances of that coming to pass are debatable.

Europe is one of the main hosts of the next tournament in 2030, with Spain and Portugal holding the majority of matches alongside Morocco, and Spain is currently lobbying hard to win the right to host the final ahead of Morocco.

There is also a women's World Cup next year in Brazil, which could be an early target for any action, if Uefa does want to take a bold step of its own.

Uefa could potentially find and field a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election, but given Uefa nations comprise only 55 votes, they would be unlikely to win.

If Ceferin and other European leaders really want to fight Infantino's plan as hard as possible, they must be willing to make a big move of some sort very quickly indeed.

For now, Infantino is as emboldened as he has ever been.

title: Have season ticket holders 'passed their sell-by date' for clubs?
description: BBC Radio Manchester's Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed restrictions on season tickets in the latest episode of The Devils' Advocate.  Manchester United has restricted the accounts of "thousands" of fans, in an operation aimed at identifying potential ticket touts.  Drinkwater said he has "full sympathy" for fans who have fallen under the restrictions despite not being involved as touts.
fullText:
BBC Radio Manchester's Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed restrictions on season tickets in the latest episode of The Devils' Advocate.

Manchester United has restricted the accounts of "thousands" of fans, in an operation aimed at identifying potential ticket touts.

Drinkwater said he has "full sympathy" for fans who have fallen under the restrictions despite not being involved as touts.

"It's pretty obvious that these were fans that were not touting tickets," Drinkwater said.

"I love that Manchester United fans have made such a massive, loud deal about this and football fans have got behind it as well because hopefully that means that these appeals will be listened to."

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire joined the podcast and gave his thoughts on why United might be taking this course of action.

Maguire said: "There's the theoretical one which is perfectly understandable. There's an awful lot of touting at Manchester United as with other big clubs - Liverpool are similar, Arsenal are similar, Chelsea and so on. There's a lot of people making a lot of money through the resale of tickets.

"The other issue is that season ticket holders, to a certain extent, have passed their sell-by date as far as the senior people at the club are concerned. If you're a local Red and you're going 19 times a season to Old Trafford, you're not going to the merchandise 19 times a season.

"You're paying high but not excessive prices for your ticket and those tickets could be repackaged by the club and they could send you to a warehouse in Trafford Park and give you a pie and a pint before the match and get a former player to tell a few anecdotes and they could sell those tickets for £200-£300 a pop. That's what the club wants."

On how the club can manage the situation without upsetting the loyal fans, Maguire said: "There's no easy way around this. Nobody is denying that touting isn't a problem at the club but the way that they have taken [to deal with it] has been quite unpleasant."

title: Five things we've learned from first half of F1 season
description: BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson analyses the five key things we've learned from the 2026 season so far.
fullText:
Formula 1 teams head off on their summer break this week after a hectic 11 races to start a new era of the sport.

F1 2026 has been full of storylines - controversy over new rules, a new star emerging, the rebirth of an old one, and calendar disruption caused by a war.

Even now, as they head off on holiday for a couple of weeks, the teams still don't know how many races are left this season.

But those so far have revealed plenty. Here are five things we have learned so far in F1 2026.

Kimi Antonelli started his Formula 1 career in 2025 hyped as the next generational talent - but did not live up to that billing in his maiden season.

This was supposed to be his team-mate George Russell's year.

Mercedes have delivered on the expectation they would be the team to beat with eight wins and 10 pole positions in the first 11 grands prix, and Russell dominated his rookie team-mate in 2025.

But Antonelli took a gargantuan step in development over the winter and, while Russell started the season strongly with a win, the Italian soon took control.

Initially, the competitive picture between the two was slightly clouded by some poor luck for Russell in the opening races of the season.

But, as time has passed, it has become increasingly clear that Antonelli is dominating his team-mate so far this season in the best car.

While Russell has floundered a little, less comfortable with the car, and is still afflicted by bad luck, pace seems to flow from Antonelli so easily. Along with devastating pace, his driving is decisive, committed and cool.

The 19-year-old will be tough to stop in the second half of the season.

Russell proud of resilience after string of problems

This year's F1 championship introduced the biggest rule change in the sport's history, with new aerodynamic and engine regulations.

While the chassis rules have generally been a hit - even if the cars are a little slower than last year - the new engines most definitely have not.

The nominal 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power (more like 53-47 in reality) combined with the architecture of the engines, has left them energy starved.

And when the battery is empty, the cars have only about 540bhp - less power than a Formula 3 car, but with loads more grip.

The need to constantly charge the battery has neutered many of the best corners on many of F1's greatest tracks, reducing them to what Fernando Alonso has called "charging stations".

The flip side is the energy starvation has led to some interesting battles, known as "yo-yo racing", with cars swapping positions repeatedly over a number of laps.

But the drivers point out this is artificial, and that overtakes are often happening simply because one driver suddenly has 350kW (470bhp) more than the other.

As four-time champion Max Verstappen says: "Sometimes people say: 'Ah yeah, but this was a great race.' I say: 'Yeah, but it's not really realistic the way we are racing.'

"And then you arrive to some tracks and you're driving on not a lot of horsepower for F1 standards. And it's a little bit painful, which I could see coming already for years. So, it's then, of course, not the most exciting.

"At one point I'm also a little bit fed up with repeating myself, because it's already hard enough just having to drive it."

The drivers - especially Verstappen and Fernando Alonso, but most of the others, too - were very vocal about this from very early in the season. The sport as a whole recognised there was a problem, and has reacted.

Tweaks to the rules to lessen the problem were made after just three races, and the engine split will be modified to become 60-40 by 2028, with an intermediate step for next year.

That will significantly reduce these issues, but not eradicate them completely.

F1's governing body the FIA was warned repeatedly in the years leading up to 2026 that this energy starvation issue would happen.

This has left an easy target for FIA president, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, to propose a return to naturally aspirated V8 engines for 2031.

It's an idea with distinctly limited support among F1's stakeholders. It lacks imagination and analysis, comes with its own set of problems, and is effectively turning the clock back 15 years.

The issue is not hybrid engines or turbos per se; it is the lack of energy recovery possibilities.

It's a situation F1 forced on itself by removing the MGU-H, which recovered energy from the turbo and exhaust, and not allowing recovery from the front axle.

The sport needs to take a pause, intelligently and rigorously analyse what it wants from its engines in the future.

Then it needs to come up with a package that satisfies the manufacturers, has road-relevance, embraces concerns about the climate crisis, does not create a noise-hazard threat to some of the sport's most high-profile races, is cheaper, allows the drivers to almost total access to full power, and gives a facility for overtaking.

Lewis Hamilton's career reached its lowest point in 2025, during a maiden season with Ferrari the seven-time champion himself described as a "nightmare".

Hamilton's struggles - in the context of a difficult final season at Mercedes in 2024 - raised all sorts of questions.

He has admitted he doubted himself at times last year.

Hamilton said: "There were definitely moments that I was like: 'Sheesh, maybe it is true that, you know, when you get to a certain point, you lose it.'"

Those comments came in the wake of his victory at the Spanish Grand Prix - the zenith of a first half-season that has definitely proved he has not "lost it".

Hamilton, 41, is rejuvenated this year - back to something close to his best - and the battle with team-mate Charles Leclerc - pretty much entirely one-sided in 2025 - is neck and neck.

He's even sort-of in the championship fight - in second place, 50 points behind Antonelli.

Is this down to the new cars behaving more to his liking than the ground-effect ones of the past four seasons, assiduous work behind the scenes to integrate himself more closely with Ferrari, or the team accommodating some of his preferences into the car design this year?

Even, as his former team boss Toto Wolff has said, "maybe the new girlfriend helps" - a reference to Hamilton's relationship with American media personality and businesswoman Kim Kardashian.

There is still some room for improvement - four penalties in the past three races is very much not Hamilton-esque. But his revival is a relief - for him, and all those who have witnessed his incredible career so far.

On paper, Aston Martin have the ingredients to be title contenders - design legend Adrian Newey in charge, multiple championship-winning engine manufacturer Honda providing the power-units, the legendary Alonso in the cockpit, and ample funding from billionaire owner Lawrence Stroll and Saudi Arabian sponsorship.

But the first half-season of this much-vaunted package has been nothing less than an embarrassment.

Both car and engine were a long way from competitiveness at the start of the season, Stroll was almost in tears when the team's predicament became clear in pre-season testing, and they spent the first 10 races right at the back.

The final race before the summer break, however, provided real hope.

A massive upgrade package based on lessons learned in the early races - increasing downforce and reducing weight - has taken what looks like two seconds off the car's lap times.

Most importantly, the success of the package proved out the team's development tools, which for the past three years had produced upgrades that did not deliver what the team expected.

A new Honda engine is due for the next race - the Dutch Grand Prix on 21-23 August - with expectations it should edge the team forwards a little more.

After the team proved it could improve the car, a lot rests on that engine. "No pressure," as Alonso himself said with a smile after Hungary. It was both a joke and not a joke.

Alonso, 44, is out of contract at the end of the year, and wants to see evidence that Honda, which has finally brought all the expertise behind its championship-winning engines with Red Bull back into the F1 design team, is on the right path.

If it's a step forward, it should significantly increase the chances of Alonso staying for another year - although he still has to convince himself he can enjoy his racing with these engines he dislikes so much.

Alonso optimistic about Aston Martin upgrade - will it decide his future?

For three years after taking over as Williams team principal at the start of 2023, James Vowles had been talking up 2026 as the year the team would make a giant leap towards their ambition of returning to winning ways.

A surprisingly strong 2025 - in which Williams finished fifth in the constructors' championship - seemed to be proof the team were not only on the right track, but even ahead of schedule.

This year, they have had a brutal reality check.

The car was late, overweight by about 25kg, and lacked performance. Williams' first half-season has proved them to be ninth fastest team and nearly 0.4secs on average slower than the team just ahead of them - Haas.

Only troubled Aston Martin and newcomers Cadillac have been slower - and Aston Martin's Hungary upgrade seems to have left Williams as the 10th best team.

And all that with the best engine on the grid - the Mercedes.

Drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon are definitely not impressed - although they continue to say the right things in public.

Vowles has explained the complexities of producing a new car to a new rule set stress-tested the factory and exposed weaknesses that were previously not apparent.

But he said similar things when the 2024 car was late.

Vowles says he's "glad" they have gone through this and insists the team are now making progress.

"Never let a good crisis go to waste," he says. "The amount of changes we have made have put us into a very good situation in the future, and I don't think we would have made them if we'd partially succeeded this winter.

"So, as painful as it's been, I believe we had to go through it as well."

title: Why can't Draper play & why won't surgery help?
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team explains the injury which has derailed former British number one Jack Draper's career over the past year.
fullText:
Former British number one Draper withdrew from a planned comeback in Washington on Monday after feeling more discomfort from bone bruising in his serving arm.

It is a similar situation to what happened at Wimbledon last month, where the 24-year-old Englishman also spoke positively about his fitness - and seemingly practised well - before pulling out on the eve of the tournament.

Draper continues to insist "finding acceptance and being patient" remains the key - but his fans can be forgiven for fearing the worst.

So what is bone bruising in the arm, how does it affect tennis players and would surgery solve Draper's long-standing issue?

Draper has been hampered by the bone bruising in his left arm for more than a year, playing just 14 matches in the past 12 months and missing all three Grand Slam tournaments so far this year.

He has dropped to the cusp of the world's top 150 as a result and will need to come through qualifying - or be given a wildcard - to play at the upcoming US Open, which starts on 30 August.

Bone bruising is essentially internal bleeding in the centre of the humerus bone, according to Prof Amar Rangan, vice-president of the British Orthopaedic Association.

The humerus is the long, tube-like bone between the shoulder and elbow joints, with the stronger outer layer - known as the cortical bone - protecting a spongier tissue called trabecular bone.

When the trabeculae break, the bleeding increases pressure inside the bone - causing bruising.

Tennis players are particularly liable to this injury because of the stresses imposed on the humerus by the rapid acceleration and deacceleration of their shots - particularly the serve.

Generally it tends to cause a dull, deep-seated pain, as well as limited mobility and inflammation for some people.

"How do you recover from this injury? A lot of patience - basically that is it," Prof Rangan told BBC Sport.

"It is almost a race between the bone healing and further stresses."

However, the notion of a player potentially needing surgery to fix the issue is emphatically rejected by Prof Rangan.

"The only thing can heal it is rest. The body has to heal and strengthen the bone," he said.

"Surgery would be further injury to the area and would not help.

"As long as there is sufficient relative rest to allow the bone to heal and strengthen and consolidate it should settle down."

Draper has leaned on other players who have dealt with the same injury, including British pair Arthur Fery and Toby Samuel.

Both players endured frustrating long spells on the sidelines, but have each come out of the other side to enjoy the best results of their careers.

Fery, 24, was a shock Wimbledon semi-finalist last month after suffering with bone bruising for most of 2024 and 2025.

Samuel, 23, is close to breaking into the world's top 100 having come back from almost a year out in 2024.

Eventually the pair felt they were able to play through the pain, but Draper remains at the stage of his recovery where he is happy to continue taking extra caution.

"It is a tough injury because there's no set time or magic cure for it," Samuel told BBC Sport.

"At first it was tough to play again. I was still feeling pain and not playing amazing. But I came through it and I haven't looked back."

Since first becoming aware of the problem in May 2025, Draper has taken a series of measures to alleviate the issue.

Initially he tried to play through the discomfort, before withdrawing from last year's US Open before his second-round match and swiftly deciding to curtail his 2025 season.

Draper opted not to play this year's Australian Open in January, then missing the French Open and Wimbledon as he continued to take precautionary moves.

Another tactic saw Draper switch to a platform serve - standing with his feet slightly wider throughout the motion to allow a smoother transfer of weight - which put less load on his arm but "didn't necessarily help" his knee, which he injured at the Barcelona Open in April.

Spending more time in ice baths, saunas and red light therapy has also become an important part of his recovery.

"You start looking into all things when you have this type of injury," Draper said at Wimbledon last month.

"I definitely looked more into my sleep and nutrition. I always did these things pretty well, but it's probably now an elite level.

"I think that will help the longevity of my career hopefully - going through this experience now."

title: Could Leeds move help Trafford challenge for England keeper spot?
description: BBC Sport examines how James Trafford's England chances could be affected it he completes a big-money move to Leeds.
fullText:
Since the 2018 World Cup, Jordan Pickford has been a fixture in the England team.

He has kept 44 clean sheets in his 91 caps and has made 33 major tournament appearances, including two European Championship finals.

But the Everton goalkeeper will be 34 by the time Euro 2028 begins - so it is only natural for thoughts to turn to who could take over from him.

The other goalkeepers in England's World Cup squad were Crystal Palace's Dean Henderson - who was probably regarded as Pickford's understudy as he played in the third-place play-off - and James Trafford of Manchester City.

Trafford is closing in on a £40m move to Leeds United that would make the 23-year-old one of the most expensive goalkeepers in history - only Kepa Arrizabalaga (£68m), Alisson (£62m) and Andre Onana (£43m) have cost more.

This latest big-money move and likely starting place at a Premier League club will give Trafford the opportunity to showcase his undoubted ability at the top level on a more regular basis.

The reported £40m fee is one Daniel Farke appears happy to pay despite Trafford's limited game time at Manchester City last season - 17 appearances in all competitions, but only four in the Premier League.

So, Leeds would be paying for the high ceiling of a young goalkeeper whose highlights have largely come in the Championship with Burnley when he conceded only 16 goals in 45 matches.

Lauded as "world class" by his then manager Scott Parker, Trafford's 29 clean sheets and 84.47% save ratio were integral to the Clarets' promotion to the Premier League in 2024-25.

Trafford, though, is yet to fully establish his reputation at the highest level of club football.

The son of a farming family from Cockermouth in Cumbria, Trafford came through City's academy before joining Burnley for an initial fee of £15m in the summer of 2023.

However, he conceded 67 goals in only 28 matches before losing his place towards the end of the 2023-24 season.

After starring in Burnley's successful promotion in 2024-25, Trafford returned to City for £27m last summer with the hope of being Pep Guardiola's number one.

Instead, City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma from Paris St-Germain just four weeks after Trafford's arrival and he became second choice - a scenario that has prompted his potential switch to Elland Road.

If the move goes through it will mean £82m has been spent on Trafford in initial transfer fees since joining Burnley three years ago.

He has only played 32 top-flight games in total, but former Clarets boss Parker previously praised his turnaround at Turf Moor before moving to Etihad Stadium.

"There's no denying at the beginning of the 2024-25 season, there was a lot of work to do with 'Traff'," Parker told BBC Radio Lancashire last April.

"He needed to take a breath and take stock and decide where he wanted to be. There's no denying that he's a world-class keeper."

Pickford is the man in possession after helping England reach the World Cup semi-finals for only the fourth time this summer.

Thomas Tuchel spoke of his admiration for both Trafford and Henderson after he was appointed England manager in 2024.

Trafford made his England debut in the 1-1 draw with Uruguay in March but Pickford played every minute of the World Cup until the game against France, when Henderson started.

In doing so he surpassed Peter Shilton's England record of 17 World Cup appearances, ending the tournament on 19.

After England defeated Mexico in the World Cup last 16, former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said: "I think he's the first name on the team sheet. There is nobody else."

Pickford has made 14 appearances at European Championships, while he has saved four of the 14 penalties he has faced in major tournament shoot-outs, guiding England to wins against Colombia in the 2018 World Cup and against Switzerland in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024.

The former Sunderland player has been consistent over nine campaigns with Everton, winning the club's player-of-the-season award three times in a row as they battled relegation between 2021 and 2024.

The 32-year-old has played 362 Premier League games in total, keeping 98 clean sheets and saving almost 70% of the shots he has faced - including 86% from outside the box.

Over the past two seasons, only Arsenal's David Raya has kept more Premier League clean sheets.

Pickford also won the competition's save-of-the-season award for a second time last season following a remarkable reactionary stop, external from Sandro Tonali's volley to secure Everton's 3-2 win at St James' Park in February.

Comparing Pickford and Trafford directly is not straightforward because of the latter's relative lack of elite-level football. However Leeds' prospective new signing has also starred on the international stage - albeit for England's age-group sides.

He played every minute of the 2023 Under-21 European Championship as England won the title for the first time in 39 years without conceding a single goal.

In Premier League terms, even when discounting the gulf in experience, Pickford boasts an undeniable edge.

Since Trafford made his top-flight debut in 2023-24, Pickford has prevented far more goals - despite facing a higher quality of shot - and has a better save percentage.

Trafford has so far failed to prevent any expected goals in Premier League football as defined by Opta.

So while Trafford will hope his possible high-profile move will help him add to his two England caps, he has work to do succeed Pickford as the Three Lions' first-choice goalkeeper.

title: Zirkzee 'too good for role Man Utd want him to play'

fullText:
Co-hosts Gaz Drinkwater and Joe McGrath discussed which players impressed them in Manchester United's comfortable pre-season win over Rosenborg in the latest episode of BBC Radio Manchester's The Devils' Advocate podcast.

Drinkwater was full of praise for Joshua Zirkzee, who scored a "Puskas award nominee" goal in the friendly, slaloming his way past defenders and goalkeeper before tapping into an empty net.

"It was a great goal and really nice to watch," he said.

"It did kind of look like United were playing on Fifa with the difficulty [level] set on amateur. It was so slow the way it happened and there's no way a goal like that would be scored in the Premier League, but I'm not saying that to discount Joshua Zirkzee or take anything away from him. It was a lovely goal."

On Zirkzee being linked with a move away from Old Trafford, Drinkwater added: "At times, he comes on and is the exact type of player you need in a game. I like a lot of his attributes and you can tell by the way he plays that he would do very well in the Italian league.

"He plays just a little bit slower but he is really, really good on the ball. He is so slick but he needs to play in a slower league.

"He's one of those players who is too good for the role we want him to play, which is very occasionally coming on and making an impact, and very rarely starting games. I wouldn't mind if we let him go."

title: Why is Hamilton getting so many penalties? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Hungarian Grand Prix.
fullText:
McLaren's Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix from pole position, his first victory since becoming world champion.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen was second and Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli completed the podium in third.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was given a five-second penalty for speeding in the pit lane and finished fifth behind his team-mate Charles Leclerc.

F1 will now go on a summer break and return for the Dutch Grand Prix, from 21-23 August.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race at the Hungaroring.

Why is Lewis Hamilton getting so many penalties at the moment? With his vast experience, you would have thought that at least some of them could have been avoided - John

Lewis Hamilton has had four penalties in the past three grands prix, which does seem a lot for a seven-time world champion.

But just because events happen in a statistical cluster does not necessarily mean there is any kind of wider pattern behind them.

In this case, it does just seem as if it's one of those things - a series of events that can happen at any time, and just happen to have happened when they did.

The penalties are all very different.

At Silverstone, Hamilton was penalised for moving before the start, after his car jumped forward briefly and then stopped before the lights went out.

At Spa, he was given a five-second penalty for causing a collision with George Russell at Les Combes on the first lap.

And in Hungary, there was a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri in qualifying, and a five-second penalty in the race for going 0.1km/h over the pit-lane speed limit while racing Kimi Antonelli out of the pits when both stopped under the late virtual safety car.

Hamilton said on Sunday after the race: "Ultimately, the last three races have been pretty bad from my side.

"Silverstone start - we talked in the drivers' briefing the fact that they're inconsistent with this stuff. Drivers in the past have moved and not been penalised.

"We discussed that, as long as you're not moving when the last lights are on, you shouldn't be penalised. I wasn't out of my [start] box. And they agreed. So they're looking into that for the future.

"The last race, even the driver I collided with said that it was just a racing incident. I think that one was not needed. But that cost me a lot of points.

"And then the one yesterday was really just unfortunate. I take responsibility for ultimately being on track. I should have looked in my mirrors. But I thought everyone would have been at the end of the first lap. The information I got was right at the end. A communication error.

"I'll work hard to try and come back. There's still a lot of positives to take. I'm going to try and make sure I don't give them any reason to penalise me."

Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder

Complete weekend for Norris but poor result for Sainz - driver ratings

Do you think Aston Martin's upgrade could persuade Fernando Alonso to continue as a driver? - Robert

Fernando Alonso is out of contract at the end of the year and has a decision to make as to whether to stay in F1 next year.

He is 45 on Wednesday and has been doing this for 25 years. He wants to be sure he makes the right decision because, unlike the last time he stepped away from F1 in 2018, there will be no coming back this time when he leaves.

Alonso has been discussing his mindset on his future all season. In a nutshell, he has said he will continue to race, but he does not know whether that will be in F1.

He enjoys the competition of F1, but - like most of his colleagues - he is not enamoured by the new generation of engines and the need for energy management and how that has detracted from the driving experience.

He has been less clear about how the competitiveness of the Aston Martin-Honda package will affect his decision.

Alonso is a difficult person to read, and he can be gnomic when he speaks.

My feeling is he is leaning towards continuing, but only if he feels he can be confident Aston Martin will be in decent shape next year. Another year like the first half of this one - stuck at the back, racing no-one - has no appeal at all.

In Hungary, the debut of the new Aston Martin car was a significantly positive step. Alonso made it out of first qualifying for the first time this year, and the race pace was strong.

The team, it turns out, had hoped for an improvement of about two seconds a lap from the aerodynamic improvements and weight-saving, and, at least in Hungary, that was pretty much delivered. That's a remarkable step - pretty much unheard of in terms of mid-season upgrades.

It was also important because the upgrade was a proving test for the factory's ability to deliver developments that worked - which had not been the case for three years.

The next step is the new Honda engine, which will make its race debut at the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break.

The Honda is a long way behind the other power units - something in the region of of about 1.5secs per lap off the best, Aston Martin believe internally.

The impending upgrade will not narrow that gap completely. But it is hoped that it will narrow about a third of it.

This is equally important for Alonso. He will want to see proof that Honda can deliver improvement - not least because he has prior experience from his time at McLaren from 2015-17 of Honda's promises not living up to reality.

I'm told he will wait to see how that goes before properly considering his decision on his future.

The team want him to stay. Team principal Adrian Newey said at the weekend: "Fernando is an amazing driver. He brings huge amounts to the team, both in his feedback and his ability.

"So, for us, of course it's important. I'm pretty confident that Fernando is enjoying his time with us and that we will continue with our relationship."

After positive progress in previous seasons, how much longer can Williams go on without making some drastic changes as they slip down the order this year? And how much longer can they retain Carlos Sainz? - Craig

This year has been a shock for Williams.

They had spent the past two seasons talking about how everything had been focused on developing the team so it could make a big step towards the front under the new 2026 rules, and instead they have taken a big step backwards.

Team principal James Vowles did not expect it, but has said that it happened because the rules ended up stress-testing the factory and exposing weakness they did not previously know existed.

Asked why the factory was not ready, given he had been there since 2023, he says, effectively, you only know what you don't know when you discover it.

Vowles concludes: "Never let a good crisis go to waste. The amount of changes we have made have put us into a very good situation in the future, and I don't think we would have made them if we'd partially succeeded this winter. So, as painful as it's been, I believe we had to go through it."

Cynics might say they have heard that sort of thing from Vowles before - when the car was late in 2024, for example.

As for the drivers, there is no question that Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon are frustrated, but the reality is they do not have a lot of options.

The driver market is a bit stuck at the moment while everyone waits to find out what Max Verstappen does.

If he moves, though, it's unlikely that either Williams driver would be Red Bull's first choice to replace him.

Verstappen would be going to either Mercedes or McLaren and the expectation would be that the drivers he is likely to replace - George Russell and Oscar Piastri - would end up swapping.

Beyond that, there are only midfield teams available.

In Sainz's case, he turned down Audi two years ago to go to Williams, and in any case, they seem happy with their current line-up.

Alpine? Is it worth going there instead of Williams?

Racing Bulls is not an option. Haas would be below either's ambitions. Cadillac even more so - and if one of their drivers move on it would likely only be to make way for reserve driver Colton Herta.

In reality, the only viable alternative might be Aston Martin - but there is only a seat there if Fernando Alonso decides to leave F1.

There were numerous blue-flag infringements in the race, which had or would have had a decisive effect on the results. How can these situations be avoided in the future? - Juha

Usually, the drivers are warned about cars coming up to lap them in three ways - a blue-flag indicator on their steering wheel, blue-light panels trackside, and traditional blue flags.

But there was a problem with the link between the F1 timing system and the FIA race-control system in Hungary - it was dropping out and kicking back in.

That meant the system erroneously believed some cars had been lapped because they were not showing up on the correct timing loops, so it started showing blue flags when no-one had been lapped.

When this was realised, the automated blue-flag system was disconnected and the FIA relied on marshals showing blue flags or pressing the buttons that operate the blue-light panels trackside.

The teams were alerted to the problem as soon as it happened, but it did lead to the odd issue.

The most high-profile of these was Carlos Sainz colliding with Oscar Piastri as the McLaren driver came up to lap him.

This potentially cost Piastri the lead, as Lando Norris was about to pit at the time, and came out only marginally ahead of his team-mate.

Sainz received a five-second penalty for that incident, as did Haas driver Oliver Bearman for failing to respect blue flags when he was being lapped by Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

For the future, the FIA is working on an update that would calculate expected car position in the case of an irregular refresh rate from the F1 timing system.

title: NI's Olympic champions struggle on medal-less Monday
description: BBC Sport NI looks at Olympic champions Rhys McClenaghan and Daniel Wiffen's struggles as both missed out on Commonwealth medals on Monday.
fullText:
"Olympic champion is feeling rusty at the Commonwealth Games."

Those were the words of 800m freestyle Olympic gold medallist Daniel Wiffen, but they equally could have come from or been applied to his fellow Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan on the pommel horse.

It was meant to be a magical Monday for Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, with both Paris 2024 champions in action.

The expectation was that they could be the two, given their previous winning pedigree, to land NI's first two gold medals in Glasgow.

It was more mediocre than magic though as both struggled in their favourite events, so much so they did not even make it to the podium, with McClenaghan sixth in the pommel horse final and Wiffen fourth in the 800m decider.

McClenaghan was a master of his own downfall, starting slowly with his new routine and finishing in even worse fashion, but he was not too downcast by his performance and wanted to focus instead on how it was a step towards a bigger goal with the next Olympics two years away.

He said that while the routine obviously "didn't go to plan" it was "another stepping stone to what's to come" on his journey back to the ultimate pinnacle of retaining Olympic gold.

Wiffen is also building for two years' time, but he was much more self-critical, stating that he "didn't know what was going on" with his display as he was outclassed by the strong Australian trio of Sam Short, Benjamin Goedemans and Matthew Galea.

"They [the Australians] have come to play, and I haven't to be honest," Wiffen said.

"I thought I would at least be a 7:42 time coming into this [he swam 7:48.82] and honestly I just felt a bit rusty coming into this.

"I did try to push it, but I just felt my stroke was all over the place."

McClenaghan finishes sixth in pommel horse final

Wiffen finishes fourth in tough 800m final

Besides their struggles on Monday, it is easy to draw parallels between the two that stretch beyond their status as Olympic gold medallists.

They were both operating at the very peak of their powers at the end of the last Olympic cycle in 2024 which helped to yield golds for both in Paris.

Then injuries struck and hit hard last year.

McClenaghan opted to go for surgery on a troublesome shoulder problem that kept him out of action for the entirety of 2025.

The Commonwealth Games are his first major event since Paris almost two years ago.

Wiffen suffered from appendicitis in June 2025 which had lasting effects that led him to pull out of the Worlds in July last year.

While he won gold in the 1500m in the European Short Course Championships, he was third in the 800m at the same meet in Lubin.

Both are now in the position of having to use 2026 to rebuild, and a medal of any colour in their favourite events would no doubt have strengthened both their feelings of being on the way back to the very top.

McClenaghan had a simple solution to his issues: to go back to the gym to "progress even more" with the Europeans upcoming in August and the Worlds in October.

Wiffen may need to do some further self-examination to find the cure to his ails, with the "nerves" he spoke about post-race obviously not being used as fuel for good performances as he felt he was "not handling them well".

While McClenaghan will have to wait until next month to write the wrongs of his display in the Glasgow International Arena, Wiffen has a chance to bounce back quickly and in style with a medal in the 1500m final on Wednesday.

His previous silver in the Commonwealth Games came in that event four years ago and a repeat at Tollcross Swimming Centre later this week would be a major confidence boost before the Europeans in two weeks' time.

"I'm going to learn from this," Wiffen said. "Normally, when I have a bad couple of swims the 1500m brings a brighter side out of it, so we will see how it goes on Wednesday.

"I hope I can go into it with a positive mindset and see what happens. I'll hopefully come back with a medal, then I will be happy.

"The main goal is the gold in LA so we're working towards that."

title: Salah, Stones & Sancho - who are the Premier League free agents?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who playing in the English top flight last season.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season is fast approaching but there are still plenty of players yet to secure their club futures.

Whether by choice or force, contracts have been run down and career paths changed.

BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who were playing for a club in the English top flight last season.

John Stones, 32 (Last club: Manchester City)

Stones now left City after a decade at the club in which he won 15 major trophies. Picked for England by Thomas Tuchel despite recent injury issues, Stones has most recently been linked with former club Everton and Italian giants AC Milan.

Mohamed Salah, 33 (Last club: Liverpool)

Salah's last few months at Anfield were not easy as his relationship with boss Arne Slot appeared to disintegrate. Both have now left Liverpool. It was widely expected Salah would move to the Saudi Pro League once the World Cup was over but he has since been linked with a move to Turkish club Besiktas.

Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly received an offer from Qatari side Al-Rayyan.

Yves Bissouma, 29 (Last club: Tottenham Hotspur)

Mali midfielder Bissouma made just 11 top-flight appearances last season as he struggled with injury and off-field issues at Spurs. He is reportedly keen on staying in the Premier League, with Fulham said to be interested.

Stefan Ortega, 33 (Last club: Nottingham Forest)

Former Manchester City number two goalkeeper Ortega made 10 appearances across all competitions for Forest last season. A move to Greek side Olympiacos is potentially close.

Tyrell Malacia, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

A difficult four-year spell at United for the Dutch left-back was marred by injuries and long stints on the sidelines. A chronic knee issue requiring surgery kept him out for over 500 days, causing him to miss the entire 2023–24 campaign. He has made just 11 appearances across all competitions since.

Adama Traore, 30 (Last club: West Ham)

Traore was released by the Hammers in the wake of their relegation to the Championship after just six months at the club. The powerful Spanish winger has been linked with a move back to Wolves, where he spent five years.

Other Premier League players who are out of contract:

Solly March, 32 (Last club: Brighton & Hove Albion)

Adam Webster, 31 (Last club: Brighton & Hove Albion)

Joel Veltman, 34 (Last club: Brighton & Hove Albion)

Nathaniel Clyne, 35 (Last club: Crystal Palace)

Seamus Coleman, 37 (Last club: Everton)

Emil Krafth, 31 (Last club: Newcastle United)

Willy Boly, 35 (Last club: Nottingham Forest)

Bertrand Traore, 30 (Last club: Sunderland)

title: 'Give him his passport' - Hearn backs British champion's citizenship fight
description: British champion Bilal Fawaz has lived in the UK for more than 20 years but is fighting for British citizenship - his story features in a new BBC documentary.
fullText:
The UK government should be "embarrassed" that boxing champion Bilal Fawaz does not have a British passport after living in the country for more than 20 years, says his promoter Eddie Hearn.

Fawaz, 38, was trafficked to the United Kingdom at the age of 14 and has not travelled outside the country since.

The London-based light-middleweight represented England as an amateur before turning professional after receiving a work permit.

He has since become British and Commonwealth champion, but his immigration status prevents him from fighting abroad - or taking his family on holiday.

"What on earth is the hold-up?" asked Hearn.

"You want to go down to Number 10 [Downing Street] and bang on the door and say: 'Any chance of dealing with this?' It's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard.

"If you were them, you'd almost be embarrassed. Someone should look at it and go, 'What are you guys doing? Give him his passport.'"

A Home Office spokesperson told BBC Sport it does not routinely comment on individual cases.

Fawaz's remarkable story is explored in the new BBC documentary Fighting for Freedom, which followed him as he prepared to defend his British title against Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May.

Fighting For Freedom - Bilal Fawaz

Born in Nigeria to a Beninese mother and Lebanese father, Fawaz says his childhood was shaped by abuse, neglect and a persistent feeling he did not belong.

He was sent to live with relatives before being taken to London, believing he would be reunited with his father. Instead, he claims he was confined in a house, forced to work and prevented from attending school or mixing with other children.

"My best friend was the window," he says. "I could see people walking and kids outside playing, but I wasn't allowed to play with them."

After escaping, he entered the care system and received convictions for minor offences - including cannabis possession and graffiti - during his youth. Fawaz says he was a vulnerable teenager who needed guidance rather than punishment.

"I've never robbed anything," he says. "I've never beaten anyone up. I've never done anything that's atrocious.

"I was just a kid who needed guidance and I never had that. Somebody should have taken care of me and fixed my whole life before I turned 18."

Fawaz found stability at the All Stars Boxing Club in west London. He became an English amateur champion and represented England six times, but was unable to pursue Olympic qualification or accept professional contracts because he did not have permission to work or travel.

He was twice held in immigration detention and threatened with deportation before a judge ruled there were no lawful grounds to detain him. He was released and found himself effectively stateless.

Fawaz received a work permit at the age of 33, by which point many professional fighters are approaching retirement.

After turning professional he made up for lost time by beating Junaid Bostan to win the English light-middleweight title, then defeating Ishmael Davis to become British and Commonwealth champion.

"Boxing saved me," he says. "It's my addiction. Boxing gave me the feeling that I deserve more. I've worked hard. When will I get the dues and respect that I deserve?"

The documentary follows Fawaz inside the gym and at home with his family, as well as on the dancefloor during one of his regular salsa sessions.

It also explores how his childhood has shaped him as a father.

"The only way I can fill the void is by being there for my family and my sons," he says. "That's healing."

Fawaz has a British partner and British children, but says he continues to feel as though the authorities do not recognise his contribution to the country.

"I am in prison," he says. "I've been in this country for 24 beautiful years and I've never travelled. I was being used. 'Fight for us... but you're not British'. I fought for them six times as an amateur. I was bleeding in the ring.

"They don't view me as important or someone who is trying to make an honest living. I am a Commonwealth champion who can never take my belt to another country."

Fawaz is on a 10-year 'route to settlement' and will be 43 before becoming eligible for British citizenship.

Under this route, people must complete 10 years of lawful residence before applying for indefinite leave to remain. The granting of that status allows them to stay in the UK without immigration restrictions.

British citizenship can then be applied for - if relevant requirements are met.

The UK has shorter settlement routes, including five-year routes available to people who meet the requirements of certain immigration categories.

The route someone follows depends on the basis of their immigration status and their individual circumstances, including factors such as family life, work, length of residence and private life in the UK.

It is not clear whether the 10-year route was the only option available to Fawaz or why that route applied in his case.

The Home Office previously said the decision to place Fawaz on a 10-year route to settlement was not made by the department.

Without a passport, Fawaz cannot accept potentially lucrative fights in countries such as Saudi Arabia or the United States. He can, however, take up such opportunities in the UK.

He believes he could already have become a world champion had he received a passport in his early 20s.

"The government are denying him that opportunity, which is so wrong," says Hearn, who would also stand to benefit from being able to get Fawaz fights overseas.

"I could get him a big fight in America. I could get him a fight in Saudi. This is a story that resonates in any part of the world. How can you not be allowed to travel?"

title: Liverpool's centre-back situation and why Iraola must act
description: BBC Sport looks at Liverpool's issues at centre-back, and what Andoni Iraola might do to fix them.
fullText:
Two centre-backs caught the eye of Liverpool's scouting department at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last November.

Within weeks, the club spent a combined £3.5m on the pair: Senegal's Mor Talla Ndiaye and Austria's Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Under Matt Newberry, Liverpool's director of global talent, this was evidence of future planning in full flow.

Yet surely no-one inside the club would have expected the teenage duo to be the centre-back pairing for most of Liverpool's opening pre-season fixture.

With Joe Gomez forced off by injury in the eighth minute against Sunderland, and neither Jeremy Jacquet or Giovanni Leoni fit to play still, Liverpool have a problem at the heart of their defence.

Looking at the long term is one thing, but they need reinforcements in the here and now.

Even before the injury, new head coach Andoni Iraola said his squad was "very thin" defensively.

Gomez was absent from Liverpool's training session in Chicago on Sunday and an update on the severity of his injury is expected this week.

He is Liverpool's longest-serving current player but has now missed 225 games because of injury, according to Transfermarkt, since signing from Charlton in 2015.

Virgil van Dijk is the club's only fit senior centre-back. The Liverpool captain is 35 and played every minute in the Premier League last season, but he is not the force that he used to be.

The Dutchman, like Gomez, is also into the last year of his contract at Anfield. There is a possibility both players will move on next summer.

One of the reasons why Liverpool allowed Ibrahima Konate to leave on a free transfer and join Real Madrid was because they felt Jacquet, 21, and Leoni, 19, whose transfers weighed in at £60m and £26m respectively, were the best young centre-backs in France and Italy.

Perhaps they will prove inspired signings, with Jacquet in line to make his debut against Leeds on Sunday.

Liverpool will give them every opportunity to fulfil their potential, but right now, just like Ndiaye and Ndukwe, both are far from the finished product.

"We need players. It's fairly obvious," former Liverpool striker Robbie Fowler told BBC Sport in New York, where the Reds take on Wrexham on Wednesday.

"I'm very sad for Joe Gomez, who has been so unfortunate with injuries. This could have been a real chance to cement his place and for him to show that we don't need another centre-half.

"We've spent money on Jacquet and Leoni and the guidance that Joe and Virgil can give from their experience to the young lads is telling.

"We won't see the best version of the young lads yet, but you do need that experience in the squad. And yes, the manager's been on record saying that we need players and I would not be surprised if another centre-half is in that conversation."

Is 'special talent' Jacquet the future of Liverpool's defence?

From the outside, Liverpool's failure to seal a move for Marc Guehi last summer looks even more interesting now.

They have a buyback clause with Jarell Quansah, who left for Bayer Leverkusen for £35m last July, but there are no current plans for Quansah to return.

Sources stress that if Liverpool bring in Bradley Barcola, who Paris St-Germain value in excess of £100m, then there will be limitations to what more they can do in the market.

Deals for Jacquet and Victor Munoz have cost a combined £94.5m.

Without any major outgoings from Iraola's squad, there is an understanding that this summer will not be like last summer when a club record £450m was spent.

Fowler, who scored 183 times for the Reds, said: "When you look at Liverpool across the last decade, one of the problems that we've had is that the first 11 is more than capable but the argument that people have is the squad depth.

"I'm a big believer in getting the squad right because it gives everyone a lift and keeps people on their toes, knowing that if you're not performing, someone else could do the job.

"Go back to the days of Phil Neal and he'll tell you stories about how players would never want to get injured because they knew that if someone else came, they wouldn't get their place back.

"You need that mentality and I think that has a real knock-on effect on standards."

In six months from last summer through to January 2026, Liverpool agreed deals for five centre-backs who were aged 20 or under at the time - Leoni, Ndiaye, Ndukwe, Noah Adekoya and Jacquet.

It is worth noting that Ndukwe, who was impressive against Sunderland, must go out on loan this year as he does not yet meet the criteria for a UK work permit.

The long-term potential of centre-backs is not a concern at Anfield.

But experience is in short supply - a glaring gap in this Liverpool squad and one that needs to be addressed.

title: BBC Micro AI Agent Experiment
description: I built an AI agent with one mission: write code for the BBC Micro - an 8-bit computer from 1981.
fullText:
Vacation side project: build an AI agent with one mission: write code for the BBC Micro - an 8-bit computer from 1981.

Now, the BBC Micro Bot community has spent years creating BBC BASIC one-liners that express amazing creativity in under 500 characters. We did not use any BBC Micro Bot programs in this experiment, nor attempt that level of finesse, however.

Instead, our agent gives the model some context about the machine and access to a BBC Micro emulator and VLM critic of the graphics output.

Click any image to open agent output in BBC BASIC editor:

Simon Willison has been asking LLMs to write an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle since 2024. It seemed only fair to make the BBC Micro attempt it, in four colours, at 320x256. However, our harness gives the models the advantage of an emulator to run against and a critic marking each attempt.

The agent is a simple loop with feedback. We used OpenRouter to test the same harness across a fairly random selection open-weight and proprietary models: GPT‑5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Gemini 3 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemma 4 26B A4B. Plan the scene, write the program, observe what happened, fix it, repeat. Observing is two questions asked in order: did it run, and does it look right?

The model calls plan and describes the scene in text - the shapes it intends, their colours, sizes and positions as well as outlining it in pseudocode.

Then the whole program, in one reply. Every attempt is a fresh few hundred characters of BASIC, written from scratch after reading the last critique. Two smaller tool calls are available here: lookup fetches a reference page (e.g. the PLOT map, VDU codes, size tricks), and count_chars gives the canonical length, counted after tokenising, where every BASIC keyword costs one character.

run_check sends the program to the beebjit emulator for 30 emulated seconds. It returns a screenshot if the program runs successfully, or else the model gets the BASIC error message and error line (e.g. "Division by zero at line 30"). A program that crashed goes straight back to be rewritten - it never reaches the critic, because there is nothing on the screen worth paying to look at.

The Qwen3 VL VLM critic drives refinement of the image. On Kimi's first attempt of a pelican on a bicycle it said:

Thanks to this observation stage in our agentic loop, Kimi's program output image goes from a one-shot seagull to genuine pelican-ness in the subsequent iterations (above)

If the critique warrants another go and turns remain, the agent loops back. When it calls submit - or runs out of turns - the session ends, but the model does not choose what ships: the harness keeps the highest-scoring attempt of the whole run.

The driver behind this investigation was the economics of popping up a website that generated BBC Micro programs. Of course, OpenAI Codex or Claude Code with frontier models do a great job of this, it but feels like a sledgehammer to crack a nut:

The questions for me was really how efficiently we can implement it. The lowest cost inference options being free-tier AI models on the cloud, or even better (from my perspective) smaller models on the edge that could run on the local machine, even in the web browser itself. The fact that Gemma4 26B A4B was quickly able to generate executable BBC BASIC programs with some passable images makes me think this is a worthwhile avenue to pursue.

Of course there is plenty of headroom to optimize the agent itself:

If we look at the Kimi Pelican example, it took twelve model calls over 295 seconds: a long block of planning, a detour to look up the graphics ROM reference after seeing the first render, then nine write-run-look cycles. In the timeline, the emulator is the row of thin red slivers, drawn a little wider than life so they show up at all - 0.23 seconds a go, 0.7% of the session, roughly eighty times less than one model call.

title: Judge limits BBC from relitigating Jan 6 in Trump lawsuit over misleading documentary edit
description: A federal judge ruled the BBC can probe how Trump's Jan. 6 speech was interpreted but relitigating the Capitol riot is not at issue in the $10 billion suit.
fullText:
A federal judge last week drew a sharp line around President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, ruling the broadcaster can probe how Trump's Jan. 6, 2021, speech was understood by the public — but cannot relitigate the riot at the U.S. Capitol itself.

The ruling was handed down by U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett as the BBC faces continued scrutiny over a 2024 "Panorama" documentary about Trump's speech on Jan. 6.

The documentary — titled "Trump: A Second Chance?" — was subsequently labeled as misleading by critics who noticed it omitted Trump's call for supporters to protest peacefully at the Capitol. The documentary stitched together remarks Trump made nearly an hour apart during his address that made it appear as if he had told his supporters to "fight like hell" down at the Capitol — the comments were actually out of context — shortly before the Capitol riot that day.

"All of the impressions that were received by President Trump's statements on Jan 6 are at issue," Lett said at the hearing, according to reports. "The full relitigation of Jan. 6 is not at issue."

Trump, Bbc Agree On Mediator For $10 Billion Lawsuit Over Jan 6 Documentary Editing Controversy

A source close to Trump's legal team, which has accused the BBC of a "fishing expedition," said the judge's decision on that specific item was significant.

"It's important because this case is about a very limited splicing that consisted of nine seconds of a more than 50-minute speech and, rather than focus just on that, the BBC is trying to distract the judge, ultimately the jurors in this case, from that very limited scenario, and what they're trying to do is expand the scope of this case to litigate January 6 simply to take the attention off of them for their own wrongful conduct," the source told Fox News Digital.

"And so when the judge made that determination that that's not going to happen, that eliminated the primary defense that the BBC was seeking to employ in this case, which was to create a distraction, to make this case into something that was just going to be unmanageable and unnecessary, which is, 'We're going to try the whole January 6 case here.' The BBC has no standing, legal standing or any basis to bring such a defense."

Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December in a personal capacity for both defamation and for a violation of Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for $5 billion apiece, seeking $10 billion total.

At Tuesday's hearing, Trump's lawyers argued in a Miami courtroom that the president's intent and third-party interpretations of his remarks were irrelevant because the lawsuit only points to the exact words Trump used in his speech, according to Politico.

Judge Dismisses Trump's $10B Defamation Lawsuit Against The Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Story

"What matters is what he said relative to what was broadcast that he said. That's it. There's nothing more that needs to be examined," Trump attorney Alejandro Brito reportedly said.

Brito cited the written apology penned by BBC Chairman Samir Shah to Trump last year, in which Shah admitted that the documentary "gave the mistaken impression that [Trump] had made a direct call for violent action."

"He acknowledged the falsity," Brito told the judge, according to the outlet.

However, Sasha Dudding, an attorney for the BBC, noted that Shah had deemed the misleading edit as unintentional, and argued that the intent behind Trump's speech is fair game for the outlet's attorneys to investigate, Politico reported.

Dudding pointed to Trump's own denial within the lawsuit, in which he asserted that he was not responsible for his supporters carrying out the riot at the Capitol, according to Politico.

From The Hunter Biden Laptop To Kamala Harris Edits: The Long History Of '60 Minutes' Controversies

Ultimately, Lett ruled that while the BBC can delve into the interpretation of Trump's speech by his supporters, the trial will not re-examine the cause or legality of the actual riot.

The judge also determined that the BBC overstepped in some instances regarding requests to examine the findings of several investigations into Jan. 6, the outlet reported.

The issue surrounding the documentary's editing integrity comes after a report from The Telegraph revealed excerpts from a whistleblower dossier compiled by Michael Prescott, a communications advisor hired by the BBC to review its editorial standards.

The whistleblower alleged the network's documentary spliced two separate comments made by Trump nearly an hour apart on the day of the Capitol riot, which erroneously implied that the president was calling for violence from his supporters.

Legal Analyst Predicts Trump Could Win 'Considerable' Damages From Bbc Documentary Lawsuit

"We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying, without noting that the statement had been edited.

In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong."

Trump called on his supporters 54 minutes later to "fight like hell" for election integrity.

The controversy ultimately led to the resignations of BBC CEO Deborah Turness and Director-General Tim Davie last year.

What drove the majority of media attention and headlines this week was Lett ordering Trump to hand over financial information as part of the suit, according to Politico.

"All of President Trump's brand, properties and businesses are impugned or said to have been impugned. Reputational, economic damages, all of that is now at issue in this case," Lett reportedly said.

Ex-bbc Director General Tells Network They Shouldn't Agree To Pay Trump Any Money

Lett reportedly based the ruling on Trump's argument that his businesses were negatively impacted by the network's coverage, thus presenting the opportunity for the BBC to delve into the financial records of over 400 companies controlled by a Trump family trust.

This was widely covered as a significant blow to Trump. Headlines included MS NOW's "BBC to access Trump's financial records as his dubious lawsuit starts to backfire," The Daily Mail's "Trump suffers humiliating legal blow in $10 billion BBC lawsuit," and The Guardian's "Trump must divulge financial details about businesses in $10bn BBC lawsuit."

However, a source close to the Trump legal team says the judge's order is "far more limiting" than what's been reported, saying she still must enter an order specifying what she'd require as part of the discovery process.

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

"The judge made it abundantly clear that although she's going to require certain financial information to be disclosed relating to the trust and the companies that are operated by the trust, that's not as broad as the BBC would like," the source told Fox News Digital. "At the end of the day, the financial information that they're seeking with regard to the Trump Organization has nothing to do with this case … We simply are viewing this in a way that's going to be far more narrowed and tailored than what's being reported."

Trump's team is now arguing he's only seeking amends for damage to his reputation rather than to businesses under his umbrella.

"This case is not going to be about any damage caused to the Trump Organization. It's always been about the damage caused to President Trump," the source close to Trump's team said.

While Lett reportedly said she does not possess the power to drop the business damages allegations from the suit, Trump can appeal the decision to one of his own appointees, U.S. District Court Judge Roy Altman.

The BBC, meanwhile, has argued the case should be dismissed on the grounds that a Florida court has no jurisdiction over what the British broadcaster aired across the ocean.

Fox News Digital reached out to the BBC for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital's Brian Flood contributed to this report.
